And why not first [mention] the whole of that place as it is?

29. On the matter of the Son of God being the 'judge of living and dead' providing forgiveness of sins, and that 'in no other is salvation'. 29.1 For He himself is 'the judge of living and dead', that is, of the righteous and the sinners, the one providing forgiveness of sins to those believing in his name and saving us by his own glory and gift.

29.2 And 'in no other is salvation', since his nature is propitiatory and savior, in no way inferior to the propitiating and saving God and Father, as the other scriptures exhort and indeed Micah says: 'Who is a god like you, who removes iniquity and overcomes iniquities?' (Micah 7:18).

29.3 And Peter in the Acts says thus: 'And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify, that he is the one appointed by God as judge of living and dead. By this all the prophets testify, that everyone believing in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name' (Acts 10:42).

29.4 We have him then spoken of favorably, appointed by God because of his saving incarnation, in which he came 'to seek and to save the lost' (Luke 19:10). Through which also it is written, 'for the Father does not judge anyone, but has given all judgment to the Son' (John 5:22); 29.5 but as a judge having been removed from the created things.

29.6 For the creation does not judge, but is subject to law and judgment. 29.7 And again: 'This is the stone which was rejected by you, the builders, and has become the head of the corner. And in no other is salvation' (Psalm 118:22).
29.8 But also the second [letter] sends universally, having this among other things about him: 'how all things of his divine power are toward life and piety...'

Since a special glory and virtue have been granted through the knowledge of Him who called us, through which the greatest and most precious gospels have been granted to us, so that through them we might become partakers of the divine nature. Therefore also James, in general terms, said: 'One is the lawgiver and judge, who is able to save and to destroy' (James 1:17).

What, then, is the need for a multitude of scriptures for this? And the Samaritans, according to John the accurate divine seer, being men of good discernment, who did not reject the voices: 'For we ourselves have heard and we know that this is truly the Savior of the world, the Christ' (John 4:42), who says, he says, gently: 'Be of good courage, child, your sins are forgiven you' (Luke 7:50).

Concerning the revealing of the Son by the Father through the equality of the Trinity and drawing us to Him, and again the Son and the Holy Spirit presenting us to the Father. In the same way also concerning the confession of Peter, and that it is repentance.

For so that it might be demonstrated through all things the equality of the blessed Trinity regarding all things, the Father reveals to us His own Son and draws us through Himself to Him and admits us into His kingdom; and again the Son and the Holy Spirit present us to God and Father. For God would not have transferred us into a different substance or a greater, nor into subordinates like His own scepter.

Therefore the new [covenant] has fulfilled the old through the faith into the Son and the divine Spirit. And thus the God the Father says in Isaiah to the Son: 'Behold, those who come near shall come to you through me, and they shall reside with you, and upon you they shall take refuge' (Isaiah 60:3); and the Son in John: 'No one is able to come to me, unless the Father who is in heaven draws him, and I will raise him up on the last day' (John 6:44).

And again, regarding Peter saying, 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God' (John 11:27), he said: 'Blessed are you, Peter, son of Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in the heavens. And I say to you, that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the heavens, and whatever you shall bind upon the earth shall be bound in the heavens, and whatever you shall loose upon the earth shall be loosed in the heavens' (Matthew 16:17-19).

before: How great is the faith and the confession that the true Son is God and not a creature, the only-begotten God the Word.

Peter did not hesitate seeing God indwelling on earth in flesh and blood; for this is that 'flesh and blood did not reveal to you' (Matt 16:17). He recognized the consubstantial and participating branch of God; in this he honored the root which was revealed to him, [being] self-begotten and unoriginated; he believed in his unity with the Father regarding divinity. He was made blessed by the only blessed Master. The churches were built upon this rock, whose 'gates of Hades' (Matt 16:18)—that is, the arguments of heretics—did not prevail; the keys of the heavens were handed to him, so that for those believing—as Peter himself seems to answer perfectly and as he heard from Christ along with the other apostles: 'baptizing them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' (Matt 28:19)—they might be opened in the kingdom of God; but for those not thus glorifying the tri-blessed and most desirable entrance, he shall shut it.

For by this, by which he was made blessed, he himself accepted this glory, whereas those speaking against him were caught and cast out. Having truthfully confessed him as the Son of God, that is, genuine and consubstantial, he heard something nearby: 'Bar Jonah', which is interpreted: 'Son of Jonah' (Mark 8:29). Peter was by no means of a different substance to the one who begot him. Along with these things he received authority, and rather all through him, not to forbid those stumbling, but to receive those repenting. For no one is without sin, except he who permitted this authority to Peter, for this is: 'whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in the heavens' (Matt 18:18). He then cast off the inhumanity of Nauatus and Sabbatius.

And Paul, writing to the Galatians, follows these things: 'But when God, who set me apart from my mother's womb, was pleased to reveal his Son in me' (Gal 1:15); and to the Colossians: 'giving thanks to the Father, who has qualified us for the portion of the inheritance of the saints in light, who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom...' (Col 1:13).

Therefore, 'the redemption, the forgiveness of sins' (1 Cor 15:22), and to the Corinthians: 'God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord' (1 Cor 1:9), and to the Ephesians: 'and having come, he preached peace to you, the distant and peace to the near, because through him we both have the access in one Spirit to the Father' (Eph 2:17-18).

Concerning the fact that there is no end to the kingdom of the Only-begotten. And so, to be ashamed of heretics saying that after the general resurrection the Son is to hand over the kingdom to the Father, [he] proclaims that the power of the Son is without end, in this way: Gabriel, being announced by Luke regarding the Theotokos: 'and the Lord God will give to him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Israel forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end' (Luke 1:32-33), says. before: His. But the Holy Spirit of God authoritatively presides over prophets and apostles, as God and Lord, as it is shown in the preceding chapters. That creation is strengthened by the all-pervading and all-powerful divine strength, and not that it strengthens itself. For it received power which endures in itself, and it does not fail to impart [this] to its fellow-servants.

And the Spirit of God strengthens through his generative, nourishing, and inexhaustible power, because he is a creator and not a creature. For the Savior says in the deeds: 'But you will receive power, upon the coming of the Holy Spirit upon you' (Acts 1:8). Just as without his coming, there is to us no power or hope toward God. And it must be understood by this, first, that the presence of the Holy Spirit signifies that [he] has come by authority; second, that he did not come as a mere messenger, but was foretold by him, the great God and Savior. And again therefore he says: 'But you sit in the city, until you are clothed with power from on high' (Acts 1:4/1:8). And this was [the power] of the Holy Spirit.

And Paul writes to the Romans, which is to be wondered at or interpreted worthily, especially from an attack, not nothing pleasant: 'I have therefore confidence in Christ Jesus toward God. And the communion of the Holy Spirit,

Participating in nature with the Father and the Son, it participates in all things, and even in being without falsehood. Creation has nothing called truth, because there is one divine truth, just as holiness and goodness are one, to which each of us used to reach, we confess.

And the Holy Spirit is foretold as truth just as the Father and the Son, because it is of the same one divinity, having nothing manifold or disagreeing. 28.1 For those having hymned about him differently, demonstrating to us his divinity and his perfect presiding over his own works, teach that he is the provider of every good and a light that is good-looking and good-making and an intellectual sun, by whom the eyes of the unerring and receptive souls are made brilliant by the light from himself, and leading them into an inward contemplation and making them see things which they had not previously seen through sin by themselves, or even making the whole complete man light-like, just as the sun makes the bodies in which it arises sun-like; and furthermore, that he also is an unexhaustible and all-sufficient healing and 'treasure of wisdom and knowledge'.

before: To have been begotten of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, as has been said, the pre-eternal and pre-cosmic Spirit of God was present with the Creator of our nature from the beginning, not as one needing help, but with identity and equality of divinity and will, just as light is not severed from light. Therefore, Macedonian, establish this with the holy ones: they do not call the divine Spirit a creature, but say it proceeds from God as His Spirit according to nature; or, as is your custom to assert, that it is inferior to God by nature and superior to angels, having received a middle nature and rank—prove that they have spoken thus; for those things have been justly honored by the God of yours and of Arius. And not as the law of art and sophistry gives, since you have dared to leave your own words against the divine Spirit; for its divine nature, even if you had the eyes of the intellect so many and such as the Scripture gave to the cherubim, you would have been able to behold it, how much more so. For who can grasp the invisible and uncontainable divinity? Or, recognizing your own impiety, you stand apart from the first ones.

But let us return again to the hypothesis from the beginning, that it sanctifies and justifies, as we said before. That it provides salvation, and provides salvation even to those who fall; which is the sole property of the almighty essence. For without God, to do anything created is impossible. 'Nor even as to grape-harvesting with eyes circling.' For the apostle said to the Philippians such things: 'For I know that this will turn out for my salvation, through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ' (Phil 4:19). Just as it is hymned concerning the Father in the Psalms: 'But not me, you shall not know; and saving, there is none besides me' (Ps 135:6); and concerning the Son in the Acts: 'And in no other is salvation. that it frees from death and forgives sins, because the immortal and propitiatory [Spirit] bears fruit from the paternal root of essence. But it is not possible for a creature to be either sinless or one of these two things by its own nature. For none of the spirits, as has been shown, is sinless; nor perhaps, exceeding the word, is the non-existent rational [being]. For the heaven itself and the sun are not blameless in regard to the purity of God.

For even if they appear at times to have done such a thing as apostles, they did not succeed by their own power, but by that of the one who said: 'In my name you will do greater things than these' (John 14:12); and by that of the Spirit of the Father who spoke in them, as Paul teaches the Romans: 'For the law of the Spirit in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and of death' (Rom 8:2). And the Master, through John, giving to us the Holy Spirit, who had lost us through the ancient disobedience, breathed into the faces of the disciples and said: 'Receive Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven; if you retain them, they are retained' (John 20:22-23). Here is so much of the authority of the unremembered Spirit: that it itself through itself forgives sins, and in its name and in its power the apostles and all who believe in it provide remission of sins.

For that only God forgives sins, glorious sayings of God indicate: 'I,' for he says, 'am he who wipes out your sins' (Isa 43:25), and: 'If your sins are as scarlet, I will make them as white as snow; if they are red, they shall be like wool' (Isa 1:18). That it works together with the Father and the Son; and that Christ performed signs and wonders and cast out demons through the power of the Spirit.

For regarding the words of the only-begotten Son, the divinely inspired Paul, writing to the Romans, clarified thus, having said: "For we shall all be presented at the judgment seat of Christ, just as it is written: 'I live, says the Lord, that every knee shall bow to me and every tongue shall confess to God'" (Rom 14:11).

Similarly, the theologian John said in the Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. All things came through him, and without him did not become one thing that has come into being. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it" (John 1:1-5). And in the Revelation: "The one who is, and who was, and who is coming, the Lord our God, the Almighty" (Rev 1:8).

The "the one who is" signifies the eternally existing divine hypostasis, just as we have said elsewhere. For the expression is indefinite, whence God said "the one who is" as his own name. The "was in the beginning" makes pre-existence [pre-existence] and makes very clearly the absurdity and falsehood of "was when he was not." For the word "was" is absolute. But in the Roman style, the absolute consists of two words; [unintelligible], it is interpreted: more than perfect. So now it is required to conceive him as supra-temporal or unoriginate. For if anyone were to say that the one who was not in the beginning, he was once an uncaused beginning. And again, how can time, which was not yet being, be a measure for the one who made it to be? "Was with God" presents that which has a Son.
Regarding God the Father, the indwelling of nature, and that from which he was—if it is proper to say so—the self-begotten Father, the Son from him co-exists with him.

The phrase 'was with God' (John 1:1) should be understood robustly, that according to God he was without beginning, unbegotten, uncontained, good, immortal, and all-ruling. For if he does not possess this regarding the overflowing wisdom, he will not possess it regarding the source from which the wisdom flows. But he possesses it regarding both. For the Word of John is manifest, certain, and unsearchable, looking only toward the divine. The phrase 'was God the Word' (John 1:1) establishes that the Word is of the essence, and that he is such a God as that Word is; and again, the uncaused. The phrase 'all things came through him, and without him nothing came into being' (John 1:3) demonstrates him, as has already been said, not merely as creator, but that he was not even created. before: Having appeared from a private opinion to be unproven, ungracious, and reckless, neither the Scripture saying that the Divine Spirit is a beginning, nor the Scripture euphemistically calling it 'Spirit of God' and 'from God' and 'divine' and 'holy', nor the Scripture not distinguishing between the first and the second regarding the nature of the divine hypostases, what dispute remains concerning them being in the unbegotten one Godhead and equality? [The opponent claims] that it fills the inhabited world and pervades all things, and that nothing created fills the inhabited world or pervades all things, and it is found in all; but rather it is the limit of the noetic powers and a defined quantity; for only these are proper to the Godhead.

But the greatness of the Holy Spirit is indissoluble, infinite, and everywhere, and through all, and in all always; filling the world and pervading according to the Godhead, yet uncontainable according to the power, and measuring indeed, but not being measured. 'For God does not give the Spirit according to measure,' as the Savior says in John (cf. John 3:8); and according to Wisdom, having [it]: 'For you love all existing things, and you loathe nothing of what you have made; for you would not have fashioned something if you hated it. How then would anything remain, if you had not willed it or if it had not been preserved by you? And spare all things, for all things are yours, O life-loving Lord, and your incorruptible Spirit is in all' (Wisdom 11:24-26). From this we appropriately name God the Father of all, not being our father by nature, as the Only-Begotten is.

And again: 'The Spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited world, and the one pervading all things has the voice of knowledge;' (cf. Ps 104:30) instead of [saying] that it has taken up the invisible and visible creation, the intelligible and sensible, and nothing of all things is without his eternal oversight; for this pervading of all things demonstrates it. And he says, it hearkens to the voice of all, as God always being in all and everywhere, and bringing every material disorder into the proper order, and being sparing toward those made by him.

And even while attending to it, since He Himself is providence and wisdom by nature, having been permeated through all things, just as the Father is. For who possesses such knowledge? Isaiah says thus: 'spirit of knowledge and reverence' (Isa 11:2), and David suggests: 'where shall I go from your face? and from your spirit where shall I flee?' (Ps 139:7). And the Lord, teaching that the divinity of the Holy Spirit is not circumscribed by place, but is simultaneously in heaven and upon the earth, always providing all sufficiency and providing to creation, said according to John: 'if you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that the spirit of truth may be with you, which the world cannot receive, it neither sees it nor knows it; but you know it, because it remains with you, and in you it shall be' (John 14:15-21).

In order that it might become known, how such testimonies manifest one single infinite nature present everywhere; they delivered the same things concerning each unmixed hypostasis: Jeremiah, explaining from God and the Father, says: 'I fill the heaven and the earth, says the Lord' (Jer 23:24); David, singing about the Son in the 40th Psalm: 'and of his greatness there is no end' (Ps 72:5); and Paul, preaching about the same: 'he is the one who descended and the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things' (Eph 4:10).

And Isaiah: 'The Lord is a good judge to the house of Israel' (Isa 30:18).

Because also the Holy Spirit of God is good, the one mentioned by David in Psalm 143 sings: 'Your good Spirit shall lead me in a level land' (Ps 143:10). In addition to these, if the eternal life and the words of the Son are good—for He said: 'I am the life' (John 14:6), and again: 'The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and are life' (John 6:64)—and if the sanctification of the Holy Spirit and the energy in the illumination are good (for it is remembered as a co-worker), and also the distribution of the heavenly gifts, then the Son and the Holy Spirit are in every way good.

We were not taught by hearing alone, but we have also seen how the distinct properties of the hypostases of the incorrupt and consubstantial Trinity enter in: of the Father from heaven saying: 'This is my beloved Son' (Matt 3:17), of His Only-begotten being baptized on earth, and of His one and only Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove and remaining upon Him, the Only-begotten God and Son. For a Davidic treasure is confirmed in this Psalm, that the one incarnated from among our wombs was attested as Son by God the Father. And the word is known to all, having here: 'Truth has risen up from the earth, righteousness has bowed down from the heavens' (Ps 85:11).

Likewise, because there is no difference in deity, the words sometimes manifest the Father with the Son in the awesome and unblemished Trinity, as when David says: 'The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand' (Ps 110:1), and Paul: 'Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ' (Rom 1:7). And sometimes they join the Father with the Holy Spirit, as when Haggai prophesies: 'For I am with you, says the Lord of hosts, and my Spirit has stood in the midst' (Hag 2:4).

"of you", and again: "not in great power nor in strength, but in my spirit," says the Lord Almighty (Zechariah 4:6). It must be applied to the word. For since the heretics, while the Spirit is being mentioned with the Father, claim that an unsubstantial power is being shown, the preceding word stands securely. And Isaiah: "and now the Lord has sent me and his spirit" (Isaiah 11:3); and again: "there the deer met and gave each other their faces. In number they came, and not one of them perished. The one did not seek the other, because the Lord commanded them and his spirit gathered them together" (Isaiah 65:23).

And Paul to the Corinthians: "do you not know that you are the temple of God and the spirit of God dwells in you" (1 Corinthians 3:16), and again: "the love of God is poured out in your hearts through the holy spirit" (Romans 5:5), and again: "but God has revealed to us through his spirit" (1 Corinthians 2:10). At other times they name only the Son, as when Isaiah prophesies: "and now, Lord, you are our Father, and we are all works of clay of your hands" (Isaiah 64:8); and Paul to the Galatians: "for as many as were baptized into Christ, have clothed themselves with Christ" (Galatians 3:27).

At other times they proclaim the only-begotten with the holy spirit, as when Paul writes to the Corinthians: "but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the spirit of our God" (1 Corinthians 6:11), to the Romans: "I say the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me in the holy spirit" (Romans 2:15), and again: "for if indeed the one coming preaches another Jesus, whom we did not preach, or you receive another spirit, which you did not receive" (2 Corinthians 11:4).

And at other times he reminds us of the holy spirit, as when Isaiah prophesies: "they rebelled and provoked the holy spirit" (Isaiah 63:10), and again: "a spirit came down from the Lord and led them" (Isaiah 48:16); and Paul writes to the Corinthians: "but a natural man does not receive the things of the spirit of God" (1 Corinthians 2:14). And just as Stephen declares in the Acts: "you resist the holy spirit" (Acts 7:51), and again: "we are witnesses of these words and the holy spirit" (Acts 22:52), just as we have become accustomed to say: "we alone are here and God [is also]."

before: Regarding the phrase 'unto the ages of ages.' It is not possible to hear it as it is, for those who are divided concerning the theologies of the Holy Spirit have determined this as a main point. For they lead themselves to the ends of the earth by presumption; and unmeasured passion is not accustomed to testify accurately to an investigation; nevertheless, nothing prevents one from hearing that device of theirs. For if they could, they would make it even more widely known.

Thus it is here: if something is called 'eternal' by name, it is possible to call it God, but if it is merely 'everlasting,' it is the Creator of the ages. For it is written: 'God is the maker of times and ages' (Ps 90:2), and again: 'Of old God spoke in many ways and in many manners to the prophets, but at the end of the days He spoke to us in Son, whom He set as heir of all things, through whom also He made the ages' (Heb 1:1-2). For if everything called 'eternal' must be named God, there would be infinite gods. For it is written: 'Rise up, eternal gates' (Ps 24:7), and again: 'Everlasting years were remembered' (Ps 102:17), and again: 'Like everlasting sheep' (Isa 54:13), and: 'These shall rise to eternal punishment' (Matt 25:46), and elsewhere: 'Those in the dust of the earth shall rise, some to everlasting life, and others to everlasting shame' (John 5:29).

Is then both the punishment and the shame God? See how much absurdity and impiety the shared name of 'eternal' falls into; it leaps upon and is swept along by the meanings and words of those people; but this is dissolved by these things: regarding the eternal name, as we have just remembered, the others, whatever they may be, did not come from time alone; but they also have the corruption of the nature of opinion, and their 'everlastingness' is altogether unlike the divine eternity; just as the one called holy, angel, or man, is similarly and perhaps this is to the Holy of Holies Spirit; for in the whole, holiness and eternity exist.

Pay attention, then, to what great clamor the 'eternal' is raised concerning the Holy Spirit, and that this wonderful and most uncontainable thing has been applied to Him, I say that He who through the Holy Spirit made the ages brings Himself to His own true Father on our behalf. Let them also consider that all the powers of the heavens are in the Holy Spirit, certainly as a co-worker with the ungraspable Creator; and that,

The heretics, not at an opportune time but in confusion, mentioned the eternal gates and thresholds, having said these things as a summary of what was brought forward to us in words. Let the difference be clear to them between the unoriginated and unchangeable eternal, and that which is from time and subject to change, and let it be known that this is not brief, nor is it only another beauty regarding essence, but is altogether transformed. Let it also be known that the Holy Spirit holds the eternal judgment toward God the Father, who strengthens all things, and the Son, not toward creatures. Having released the inferior opinion, let them embrace the better; and let them marvel, instead of what they do now, at what is worthy of marveling; and let them practice a better time after these things, for there is no envy. And having made themselves victims of the arrogant reproach of those things, they have thereby brought forth the benefit of repentance.

For if this word, as something indicating the divine, was used concerning God the Father and the Son, perhaps it might similarly be applied to the Spirit of God. One thing is this: another is that nothing of those things of which they remembered the eternal was decreed as divine, or a Holy Spirit proceeding from God—that is, one thing, and not a plurality; nor is it arranged with the Father and the Son for divine initiation and divine gift, nor of any other, lest I say too much, it was unworthy of the honor belonging to divinity. Other things toward this: God and Father pleased through His Son, the Word, to have all things created. And what an insult, as they dream, to His all-holy Spirit, from not being created! For if, according to them, it is not inexpressibly a co-worker with the Creator as the Father is? But since all energy and gift, creative and good and perfect, belongs to His only-begotten Son, the Word, and to the one Holy Spirit, and is common to them, all things are led up to the One, from whom these blessed hypotheses appeared inexpressibly along with Him; these things a person, having made himself a quiet examiner, full of the reasonings of wisdom, which are mentioned in various places of this book and those before it, could easily learn. And Paul, who is greater than men, left this clearly confirmed to the Corinthians: 'But you were removed, but you were justified, but...'

before: A righteous man and one fearing God, being testified to by all the nations of the Jews, was informed by a holy angel that he was to be brought into his house and to hear words from you. You indeed, if you had remained silent and had shut the mouths of slanders, would have acted much more effectively.

But we, returning toward the most perfect goal and providing this summary and cheerfulness to those about to receive [us], and instilling more of the orthodox zeal, say that just as no communion of nature exists in creation toward the uncreated nature, so also no such [communion] exists in [mere] information. For the one announces, and the other, not knowing, might be enabled to speak by the Holy Spirit, and from this he receives the name 'angel'; but the Holy Spirit, since He knows all things of God, as Paul confirms, informs divinely, just as the Father, seeing with the sleepless eyes of the deity what is willed, [informs] the Father and the Son, and not in a servile way, like a bodyguard angel. For 'the slave does not know what his master is doing' (Luke 12:47), nor can the one of the same substance [possess] the knowledge of the other being of a different substance; for to each nature, the knowledge not belonging to it and memory are co-participating in error; but even what is known by the generated nature is lost by time. Therefore, even here, the ignorant ones, rushing into the field of the battle of the Word, have gone astray.

For it is written: 'And while Peter was remembering the word, the Holy Spirit said to him: Behold, three men are seeking you. But arising, go with them, distinguishing nothing; because I have sent them.' (Acts 10:19-20). Having come down to the men, Peter said: 'Behold, I am the one you are seeking; what is the reason for which you have come?' (Acts 10:21). And they said: 'Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man' (Acts 10:24), and the following, as it is intended. So, even before good judges, the angel's informing appears to be learned from the Holy Spirit. For to foretell with certainty is a distinguished mark of deity; and this is for the good of those hearing, so that, being made secure, they might be saved. Furthermore, do you not think that by proposing such things, one is somewhat flattering the creation, or perhaps criticizing him who has adorned his own works with the words spoken about him through abundance?
And of his grace. For from this he did not insult himself at all, but rather he showed himself to be praiseworthy, and his works were habitually made bright.

We, indeed, if we carry the matter of the Holy Spirit's endowment as something of divine dignity, and it suffices by itself for testimony, yet we brought forth not only that, but also a multitude of other high and indisputable proofs; if you attend to these without contradiction, you will certainly be less speechless than the fish. Therefore Paul most clearly exposes your trickery, having written to the Ephesians: 'To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given in the Gentiles, to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ and to enlighten all, what is the economy of the mystery having been hidden from the ages in God the Creator, so that now might be known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places through the church the manifold wisdom of God' (Eph 3:8). Understand, therefore, how much the nature of the angels is lacking in knowing of itself things that are to come and in endowment; for even through this church of God in this world, which we are, they learn the great things. And toward persuasion, one can grasp something regarding this, which he wrote to the Colossians thus: 'This mystery which was hidden before the ages and from the generations, which has now been revealed to his saints' (Col 1:26). For before this, he says, it was known to God alone.

Toward these things, and also that which concerns the benefit of all men, of which I speak concerning the unchosen economy, this is raised by Peter to the rhetoricians, as it was foretold: 'Angels desire to look into things' (1 Pet 1:12), he says. And if they had any innate knowledge, they would not long to even stoop into it, but because they do not have it, they fall into a sort of excessive desire, like men, for those things whose knowledge is not above them. For it has become nature to overlook easily found things and to make the rarer things a matter of effort. And yet even this is not according to their nature, for by the common reason of their nature I do not say that all are obligated to some extent. before: "...and God was not a stranger among them." Jeremiah likewise says: "And you have not said, 'Where is the Lord, the one who brought you up from the land of Egypt, the one who guided you in the wilderness?'" (Jeremiah 2:19). (Isaiah 43:16). And Paul teaches that Christ has become their guide: "For they drank from a spiritual following rock, and the rock was Christ." (1 Corinthians 10:4). To this, Jude also writes universally: "For once the Lord Jesus, having saved a people out of Egypt, a second time destroyed those who did not believe in Him." (Jude 1:5).

There, therefore, the attempt of those who call the seventh Son and the Divine Spirit a creature is twice refuted, as is the use of 'another hypostasis' as a pretext to mark the one infinite nature as being different, and the claim that 'God was not a stranger among them,' that is to say, of a different substance. In the same manner Moses says: "There shall be no inheritance or lot for the Levites in the land; the Lord Himself is their inheritance." (Numbers 18:20). And Jeremiah says: "He who formed all things is Himself the inheritance of Jacob; the Lord is His name." (Jeremiah 10:7). And David says in the 14th Psalm: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup." (Psalm 16:5).

(1 Corinthians 12:11). He clearly and explicitly presents Him as God, consubstantial with the Father and the Son at once, and as self-determining. before: They said at his birth: 'Glory to God in the highest and peace on earth.'

A summary concerning worship. We have seen, therefore, him being glorified, we have seen him also being worshipped. Both are fitting and owed to God, not to a creature, just as the submissive saints write. David in Psalm 44 says: 'Come, let us worship and bow down to him, and let us weep before the Lord who made us, for he is our God and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand.' And in Psalm 72: 'All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him, for the kingdom belongs to the Lord and he himself is ruler of the nations.' What then will those say who assign the name 'God' separately to the Father, and 'Lord' to the Son, while they include here the Lord to be worshipped and to rule and his being the kingdom? And again in Psalm 29: 'And I will worship you, Lord, my strength.' And in Psalm 132: 'Let us worship toward the place where his feet stood.' Paul writes from the song of Deuteronomy: 'When he brings the firstborn into the inhabited world, he says: and let all the angels of God worship him.' And the evangelist says, 'the magi said: we saw his star in the east and we came to worship him.' And again, 'behold,' he says, 'a leper came and worshipped him.' And again according to Matthew he says: 'the wind ceased. And they in the ship worshipped him, saying: truly you are the Son of God,' and not, he says, those called sons by a cheap gift among us. And: 'a certain ruler worshipped him.' And after his resurrection on the mountain he says: 'the apostles, having seen him, worshipped him.'

A summary concerning faith toward God the Father. Therefore, according to the Scripture, saying much more or about the Father, [it says] much about the Son, declaring him almighty, and creator of the ages, and creator of all things, and true God, and not having a God before him, and over all, and a great and above all God, to whom no other will be reckoned, and sitting at the right hand...

Being in the bosom of the Father, and being the eternal life, the true light, Lord of all, only Sovereign and Authority, whose peace has no limit but exceeds all understanding, whose kingdom is unending, who alone is salvation, and who draws the worthy toward the Son; the Father is not considered in any way inferior—may it never be—to His Spirit.

One who theologizes about the Father in such an equal manner ought not to consider the Only-begotten or the Holy Spirit as lesser or unlike. For no creature has the power—only the Uncreated—to do the things mentioned: to create essence out of non-existence, both irrational and rational, to give life, to forgive sins, to call creation His own, to know the Father from equal things as He is known by Him, to be equal to the Father, to be in the Father and the Father in Him by equality, to be ministered to by angels, and for the Only-begotten to be testified as even surpassing these: God, Light from Light, Eternal Life, Truth, and Savior, being everywhere present and all things being established in Him, and for Him to possess the kingdom of heaven and divine peace, to grant it unshakeably to all, and to provide security in the continuous salvation to those who call upon Him.

For those who call the true Son of God and the Holy and life-giving Spirit 'creature' and 'not without a ruler' do not believe in these Hypostases, even if they say they believe; perhaps they do not even believe in the Father. For they transgress the command of the commanding Father: 'Hear, my people, and I will speak to you, O Israel; and I testify to you, if you listen to me: there shall not be among you a strange god, nor shall you worship a god other than [the true one]' (Deuteronomy 6:4, 14) instead of [the truth that] there is never a non-existent or heterousian one; and 'You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him alone shall you serve' (Deuteronomy 6:13); and 'There shall not be to you other gods besides me' (Exodus 20:3); and 'Cursed is everyone who puts his hope in man' (Jeremiah 17:5), that is, in a work of art. This is what the Son says in Matthew: 'No one can serve two masters' (Matthew 6:24), that is, two natures or two lordships; and in Paul to the Romans...

before: Again, regarding the Colossians and the Hebrews, it is written: 'who is the image of the invisible God' (Col 1:15). And in the Gospel according to John, the Son, presenting his own essence to be stamped with a Fatherly character, said: 'for this God the Father has stamped' (John 5:23).

This makes manifest the co-existence of the seal with the archetype, being of like-nature, and in itself showing perfectly and truly the unity of nature of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For the seal, just like the character, signifies that which is similar and undefiled.

Since it is a time to speak, and it is not improper or incomparable to have the Father [as the archetype], even if he is being imaged and characterized by a created and dissimilar thing. These divine things, not understanding correctly the words of unsearchable interpretation, but twisting them and contending with human thoughts against the words of God, say: 'another God and another image of God, just as another man and another image of a man.'

And in a certain way they represent the living and active God-Logos as a motionless image. But in essence and in every respect, he is an unerring and sovereign image of the Father, and not according to form and shape, like a statue carved or sculpted, breathless and not self-moving, nor according to kind and color, like an artificial and imitative silent image. For these things do not even according to nature, nor indeed in all other respects, manifest the Prototype.

For indeed the Son is an image of his own Father's essence of a man; but it happens to deviate in age or kind or mind or power or dignity or related things or something else. But the God-Logos unerringly and precisely images in all respects the simple, undivided, and unlike Fatherly divinity, naturally and sovereignly.

For it is not possible to think, as if he were an image of God according to something and deviates from something; nor indeed does he become an 'incomparable' image; nor is it possible through the dissimilar or the lesser or the subordinate that the true and archetypal and greater and self-determining and incomparable might be shown; nor again through the creature can the natural form of the creator be understood. For indeed no other nature demonstrates the other within itself. But even the Father is found to have become without hypostasis, when the heretics do not teach the character.

Not of his hypostasis. But even the invisible, uncomposed, and formless God does not possess an image such as those they claim is imitative. And he clearly dissolves their argument and their induction, saying: 'To be equal to God was not considered a robbery.' And Moses also leads forward concerning a natural image, saying thus: 'Adam begat Seth according to his image' (Gen 5:3). Yet Seth was not necessarily of a different substance from Adam, yet he called the image and likeness of the essence an 'idea'.

But also concerning man, he says, it has been written, that he is 'an image and glory of God'. But nowhere, O you [ones], has it been written that man or any other creature is to be 'an emanation of the glory of God and a character of the hypostasis'. It is something else to be a man as an image of God, that is, the thing made of the maker, just as Solomon says concerning the product of a carpenter: 'The maker is perceived in a likeness to the things created'; but it is something else to be, according to the same form and identical and co-ruling, an emanation of glory and a character of hypostasis, in-dwelling and unerring. For he says: 'He who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). But he who has seen a man has not seen God, just as he who has seen the product has not seen the carpenter.

But it is also necessary that for the only invisible God, that image is to be only invisible, and not the visible man according to the image. Therefore, the Son is not like any other: for he writes, 'Who shall be conformed to the Lord?' (Rom 8:29). Nor is he unlike his own Father: 'For I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), he says. And those who take the concept of the creator's image upon him, they resemble Nebuchadnezzar, worshipping an unconscious image made by [someone].

And God justly cast out Adam through the disobedience from the paradise; but the Son brought in the thief, and Adam with him, and the whole common race, as being altogether equal in divinity and goodness and lordship to the one who cast [them] out. Where has it been written that 'the Father is incomparable' to his own Only-begotten? Or that his Son is the creator and judge of all, according to his divine nature and the infinite nature of all things removed from them, is a 'creature'? Or altogether that at no time 'he was' (John 1:1)? Or where did the Father say privately, 'Create a son for me,' or the Son [say]?

before: To produce heaven, earth, and sea brought forth upon the water, being both life-producing and life-nourishing, is his work? In the same way, one cannot drive out the Spirit of God—which is of wisdom, power, and holiness—to be a co-creator of God, a holy one.

And what greater proof could be found for this than that it renews and sanctifies in each one through baptism the Spirit of God, and calls back to the better and first form of life? This is also shown by the fact that it itself recalls, as the apostle says concerning those becoming fit through the new birth and enjoying the greatest of all things expected in every respect: 'that you might become according to the image of the one who created you' (2 Cor 3:18); and it also prophesies David in the Psalm: 'the people being created shall praise the Lord' (Ps 22:27). If it did not have a communion of essence, lordship, and energy with the Father and with the Son, 'through whom all things came to be' (John 1:3), it would not renew and sanctify.

Therefore, with the all-holy Spirit, Christ, after the resurrection, breathing into the faces of the disciples, was reclaiming and sanctifying what was corrupted by human disobedience, and said: 'Receive Holy Spirit' (John 20:22); fulfilling the prophecy of Nahum, which relates the thing happening as if already done, through the unbridled desire for the immeasurable beauty of the matter: 'The one who breathes into your face has ascended from the earth, and is lifting you out of tribulation' (Nah 1:15).

Because that it is to create and to sanctify, which the divine Spirit is accustomed to do, David testifies, singing: 'Create in me a clean heart, O God' (Ps 51:10), that is: sanctify me, so that I might be renewed, having been corrupted by sin; for how else could another heart be created for him? And he confirms this with: 'And a steadfast spirit establish within my innermost parts' (Ps 51:12), instead of: 'Provide me a spirit of your exceeding reverence, so that,' he says, 'being revealed pure through its sanctification, I might become worthy of your temple.' For from the oversight of Him alone and of your Son, O Lord, we receive the sound of all evils and remain firm in hope.

We become for all eternal good. For it is manifest to us that David asks for himself to be inaugurated; for how could that which was already his, a spirit coming upon him just now, be inaugurated? But even greater and more necessary is what the Scripture, knowing the difference between creating and sanctifying, says concerning Judas, the merciful one who lost his sanctification: 'It would have been good for him if that man had not been born' (Ps 132:13), for, he says, Judas did the most disadvantageous thing of all, and he gave the Lord for nothing and exchanged life for silver.

And indeed, concerning the economy of the slave form in the unutterable mystery, where John says: 'And the Word became flesh' (Jn 1:14), and Paul: 'He emptied himself, taking the form of a slave' (Phil 2:7), and Solomon said: 'Wisdom built herself a house' (Prov 9:1); and Matthew, because of the same divine nature and energy, set it out thus: 'Now the birth of Jesus Christ was thus: when his mother Mary was betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found having in her womb from the Holy Spirit' (Matt 1:18-25). And the archangel said: 'For that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit' (Lk 1:35), and again: 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore also the one being born will be called a holy Son of the Most High' (Lk 1:32).

It must be remembered, therefore, that because of heretical wanderings, the evangelist preordained the incarnation, then the birth. For dragging our scriptural proofs through the ground, they say mockingly as if in hypocrisy: 'Is the Christ then a Son of the Spirit?' Truly, not even hearing these things, nor that which was said by him to the apostles: 'You do not know of what Spirit the Son of Man is' (Mk 4:40).

If, therefore, since God the Father is true, for this reason also his energy is divine in every way and in all respects; since the energy of the Holy Spirit appears equal and similar to this, for this reason also he himself proves to be true God. And it would be appropriate to say the same concerning the Son. For if the energy of the Father is not inferior to that of the Son or the Spirit—for how at all does the Spirit or the Son work in us?—even if they bring a power that acts by hand, if they are dissimilar as the heretics say; if indeed the fullness of the Son and the Spirit is useful and salvific, the [one] will be in no way dissimilar.

before: That calling him the true Son and the true Spirit denotes the appropriation of nature by God: but regarding all other things, it differs by lordship or by faith; just as we are accustomed to say regarding those who are of the same substance to us, 'my son, my spirit,' but regarding others, 'my field, my horse,' yet also 'my God.'

For the manner of the hypostatic Logos of the divine nature is not shown to have become Son and only-begotten and the Word of God, Christ, by simply and unattachedly speaking, but by having the syllable of 'my' and 'your' joined together. As when God says, 'This is my beloved Son' (Matt 3:17), and again, 'my good Word,' and, 'I prepared a lamp for my Christ'; and we say, 'your Son, your only-begotten, your Christ.'

Nor does it being called by the same name or by a similar name regarding us—'sons of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted?' For in the riddles concerning him, some declaration of his divine nature and power is always found. But the creatures received the holy and eternal toward their own nature, not possessing these things by nature from themselves.

For the Father said, 'My Spirit shall not remain in these men' (cf. Ps 105:36), and the Son: 'Receive the Holy Spirit' (John 20:22). It is clear.

For great elements indeed are heaven, earth, and sea; and a great rational creation is the angels and all the supracosmic power; but the Trinity did not deign from one of these, but has the name 'lover of mankind' from the goodness toward man.

before: Regarding this point, they say, moving all sorts of weapons against the uninstructed, and asserting snatchingly: 'Praise the Lord, for it is a good psalm; praise is sweet to God,' (Ps 146:1) and 'It is good to confess to the Lord and to sing to your name, exalt.' One should answer them thus: if you accept regarding the Father the voices you have brought forward, you cast out the Son; but if regarding the Son, the opposite, then when the Holy Spirit is also called 'Lord' and it is written, and it is unclear regarding which hypostasis it is written now, 'Lord.' As for the Holy Spirit, because he is not a creature, it is easy to learn that he is co-praised with God, both from his being arranged with Him and from the exhortation to praise all creation by name, both the three children and the psalmist; not, however, the Spirit of God, as the saints have a habit of naming. For if, as the heretics say, he is of a nature between God and angels, more honored and higher than all, it would have been necessary, since he is especially one, either to exhort him by himself to praise, or even to name him first and generally take up the others with him; not, however, as they arbitrarily imagine, the reverse, that he is named with the Father and the Son.

And regarding the heretical opposition: creation is not numbered with God. For what is common to that which exists in diminution compared to the All-Supreme and above all existing things in excess, or to the one who made it? But the all-venerable Spirit, as God, is named with the Father and the Son, as when the master gives the rule concerning baptism, and as when the apostle writes to the Corinthians the second [thing]: 'The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with all of you;' (2 Cor 13:13) or with one of them [the hypostases]; or even as a permanence, as is remembered in the first book mentioned.

From the intention of the outcast and rejected Valentinus, having become a Manichaean, and from his madly speaking with other absurd myth-making, the Macedonians say that the divine Spirit rushes toward the angels. Paul wrote to Timothy:

“I testify before God and the Lord Jesus Christ and the chosen angels.” But the Holy Spirit, as you perhaps appointed to the angels, was passed over in silence. From the abundance of their own heart, this is the concept.

For even if a memory of the Holy Spirit is not at times personally generated, it is taken up with God the Father, since it is His spirit by nature; that is, when God the Father Himself was not remembered by word, but by faithful thought, and the Son and the Holy Spirit were remembered, or vice versa. Whereas Valentinus, not being obligated to remember, called the sanctifying spirit “Paraclete,” just as the Lord Christ was called “Paraclete” from the sense of being called to one's side; but he called the sanctified ministers “angels.”

In addition to this: nowhere in Scripture do we find angels being remembered together with God for creation, or for mysticism, or for doxology. But regarding the communion of the Holy Spirit with the Divinity, Paul wrote to the Corinthians in the second epistle: “the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God the Father and the communion of the Holy Spirit” (2 Cor 13:13), and in others: “if any communion of the Spirit.”

before: Of the only-begotten deity: and from such a judgment it is shown that he himself exists by nature as holiness and goodness and power, being one out of the one. Since against their contention, neither the most good and merciful in nature shall the Son still be good; because 'one God' does not have a unified nature. Nor indeed shall the most philanthropic and entirely merciful Father and the Son possess the aforementioned names of deity; but rather through them they shall be demoted, as it is the custom to speak to heretics, to us who are homonymous. Be merciful, O Holy Trinity.

But the Son, he says, having been co-begotten, possesses goodness by nature, and all the other things that the Father has. But also the Holy Spirit, having proceeded together, is good by nature, and all the things the God Father has.

3.30 If, therefore, their discussion was about accidental or worldly matters, it would have been well for them to have need to weave certain myths, and with an Aristotelian-seeming skill and a technique in words, like Eunomius, to twist the matter and to overshadow the truth; 3.31 but now Paul teaches: 'unless you believe, you will not understand at all' (Luke 24:25), and: 'the wisdom of men is foolishness with God' (1 Cor 3:19). And the words concerning the glorious Spirit ought not to be made more wise than human reasoning. For reproach does not harm the Holy Spirit, nor furthermore from hearing do the insults and the mockeries of the heretics come, to whom the evil thought has fallen upon; but those using such things will suffer endlessly and will act similarly to those attempting to mock this light, which has its strength from the unapproachable light, and defile it with their words. 3.32 And it is necessary to believe that the teaching from the saints is able to impart more glory than that from men.

It is therefore fitting for us to take care not, through an excessive goodwill, to draw down the divine which is upon them into the results of creatures by sophistries regarding their own heresy, and through these to give birth to a love of destruction to the simpler and more ignorant, and to lead forward into a desire for greater sins.
4. Regarding those heretical ones saying: God is spirit; and how the Holy Spirit is spirit of the spirit? And again: the angels, therefore, they say, are not...

Are they from God and holy and spirits of God? But while they are being sent out, they are simple, direct, and perfect, yet they corrupt the choice of sacred words through ignorance, by which the Father God willed His Spirit to be arranged with Him, as the only-begotten Word, and His being removed from creation and exceeding [all] is secured, wherefore also He is thrice-sung, they say; how is the Spirit, the Holy Spirit, a Spirit?

For although this is written and shown; but the 'how' exceeds the knowledge of mind and word of us, and even of angels. For just as the God-Word was begotten from Him as a Father exists, so from Him and with Him the Holy Spirit was manifested; and in this especially His ungraspability is shown, in that what is appearing and being is impossible to be by Him through creation. For what is the difference between the uncaused and life-giving nature and the created and being-made-life-giving? Nor is it possible for the Spirit not to be consubstantial and equal to that from whom he is. Therefore he is also holy by nature.

The angels, he says, are they not from God and holy and spirits of God? They are from God, in that they have become under His command, as all things; but holy after being sanctified, like men; and spirits, insofar as they are incorporeal to us.

They are not called spirits of God or from God or proceeding from the Father or divine or spirits of truth or spirits of holiness; but ministering angels and heavenly bodies because they infinitely distance and subtilize themselves from the uncreated Spirit of God, according to the writer who is an experienced apostle: 'bodies on earth and bodies in heaven' (Col 1:2).

For just as the spirits of the winds are not according to them, neither are they according to the Holy Spirit of God. before: Lord: 'you alone are most high over all the earth' (Psalm 53:6), saying 'alone' because of the one divinity. He called him Father of eternity, being the creator of even the past ages, because he was known by men much more through the temporal aspect of the economy.

Therefore, he called him Father, as a creator and not of uncreated nature; for one is the Father of the uncreated and consubstantial Son. And to demonstrate his divinity, he said something simple: 'there is no limit to his peace.'

And Jeremiah, or rather, for the book of Baruch is one of both, solemnly speaks about him: 'This is our God; no other shall be reckoned against him (Isaiah 42:8). He found every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his child and to Israel, the one beloved by him; after these things he appeared upon the earth and walked among men.'

If, therefore, it is not conceived in a God-befitting manner that the present scripture was spoken thus because of the shared divinity of both the unutterable hypostases, it remains to say, effectively blaspheming, that the one who created is God and Father, but not our God, and is not comparable to his Son.

Thus, the word of those who slander has fallen away and spread, making the God the Word smaller and a subordinate. For how could another be incomparable to God, 'to whom no other shall be reckoned against him'?

And again: 'gods, who did not make heaven and earth, destroyed upon the earth; Lord, who made the heavens in wisdom, he is the living and true God' (Psalm 95:3), as if there were another divinity that is not true, except that of the genuine Son of God, through whom and from whom and by whom the heavens were also provided for the whole world.

And Paul, the preeminent of men, following the same sequence, gives words fittingly concerning him, writing to Titus: 'awaiting the blessed hope and the appearance of the glory of the great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, to redeem us from all lawlessness and to cleanse for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works' (Titus 2:13).

For through the being called 'the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ,' it is made manifest that he does not have a second-rank status in essence, and [the distinction] of the unoriginate toward the great God the Father.

For according to appearances it is possible to conclude that if the Son is small, how will the Father be great? If the Word God 'was when he was not' (John 1:1), he was when the name of the Father did not exist. Let it be gracious to us that we dare to say such things because of the ignorance of others. 'For piety is a beautiful habit', they say, 'for those using it'.

But through the saying 'of the one giving himself for us, in order that he might cleanse for himself a people of his own possession' (Hebrews 5:9)—not for another in order that he might cleanse a people—it follows what has been mentioned. For it signifies that he himself, the one single, self-possessing and good deity, who is the cause of all, has been determined. For it is a peculiar thing for a creator, indeed, not to surpass his own creation, if it must be said so of his own work; but for the deity of a beloved Son, having no difference from the Father, to acquire the people for himself.

And this great and true interpreter leads the argument to demonstrate that he is at once a philanthropic Savior God, and at once, as he himself veiled himself and did not show himself as superior in deity, to become with us as one of us, through a change and through sin, he asserts: 'When indeed the kindness and the philanthropy of our Savior God appeared, not because of the works which we ourselves did, but according to his great mercy, he saved us through the bath of regeneration and the renewal of the Holy Spirit'.

And he also reproaches the Colossians and makes a disparagement of the primary theology concerning him by the writings, as it has already been said in the chapter 'on the consubstantial': 'Why according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ Jesus? For in him dwells all the fullness of deity bodily' (Colossians 2:9), that is, essentially. For he also is by nature a fullness, the Father's deity existing in essence.

For 'being equal to God was not considered a robbery' (Philippians 2:6); but we received from the fullness because of his goodness. Which we by nature as slaves did not have, John saying: 'And from his fullness we all have received, and grace for grace' (John 1:16), that is, the grace of the rebirth instead of the grace which we were cast away from, striking at the first law given upon the single stock. before: We breathe. Therefore they hid themselves as through whom we are unseasonably not being gathered together, and the one in the beginning returns to the unchangeable home. Because they have leapt away, they drive things against the apostle, on account of his testifying in the words lying before him in the presence of the created nature and the creature, similarly to how one says: 'I have sinned against God and men,' and: 'I testify today the heaven and the earth,' and: 'Hear, O heaven, and be attentive, O earth.'

That because it participates, as in essence, so also in the names, the creation has no participation in the names toward those called names upon God, just as in the nature. But the Holy Spirit participates in the names of God because he also participates in the nature, except that the Father alone is called 'Father', because of being the only hypostasis to beget, and the Son 'Son' and not Father of a created nature, because of having been truly begotten but not having been begotten. Just as whenever the Scripture names even the Spirit itself 'Lord', as master of all and participating in the one kingdom with the Father and the Son; 'Holy', as being holy by nature and as sanctifying the creation; 'Incorruptible', 'Good', 'Love', 'Wisdom', 'Understanding', just as he also has characterized God; 'Power', from which he strengthens; 'Just', from which he justifies, being self-righteous; 'Paraclete', just as the Son; 'Fire', from which he appeared to the apostles in tongues of fire, just as Moses says concerning the Father: 'Our God is a consuming fire,' and concerning the Son John says: 'He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire,' and so many such things.

That he is one and not many, like the creatures. The creation does not have anything existing in one hypostasis, that is, in one person. For angels and archangels are many, the seraphim likewise, the cherubim are not one thing; principalities and powers are said, dominions and thrones; heavens in the plural, men and the rest of the creatures. For the sun and the moon participate in the multitude of the stars both in nature and in the fire-like form, as the first more actively encompasses this, as the word explains. But the Holy Spirit, as not being numbered among the creation, the words have made it clear to us that he is one and the same. That because of being consubstantial and without beginning, it has been written to be the water of life.
Having proceeded from the paternal source. Creation is not written to be the water of life, for it did not possess eternal life from itself, unlike the unoriginated, living God.

But the holy Spirit—as the preachers to be mentioned in the footnotes say—is this being one proceeding naturally from the undying and life-giving paternal source, not being created. Just as in the first word we said that light does not create its own radiance but begets it, so it is here: the source does not create the water from itself, but it has it proceeding and being consubstantial; for no one is the creator of himself, or of a son, or of a spirit, since he would no longer be a father, nor possess a spirit.

Jeremiah, in the person of God, says: 'The heavens were out of joint at this, and the earth trembled at this: because my people have done two evil things. They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have hewn for themselves broken cisterns, which cannot hold water' (Jeremiah 2:12). The prophet mystically sets forth the mystery. For he called God 'a fountain' and called the holy Spirit 'living water,' who in the baptismal pool cleanses all our sins, being unable to be split apart by the nature of the intellectual fountain, just as a stream from fountains cannot.

Isaiah says similarly: 'I will give water in thirst to those going in no-water; I will pour my spirit upon your seed and my blessings upon your children; and they shall rise up in the midst of water like grass, and like a willow tree beside running water' (Isaiah 44:3). And this contains an intellectual division through hidden things. For those in ignorance, he says, happen to receive the baptism, and because of this, 'those going in no-water,' 'I will pour my spirit' is able to make the baptismal pool overflow upon them like the sprouts of plants, and: 'like the tree planted by the outlets of the waters; which will give its fruit in its season, and its leaf will not wither' (Psalm 1:3).

And the Psalmist, doing what is necessary to make the truth apparent through words, recalls in one psalm: 'for with you is the fountain of life' (Psalm 36:9), and in another: 'he sends his word and shows them; he sends his spirit and waters flow, rejoicing the great city of God' (Psalm 147:15); and this is the whole inhabited world. For so that I may say, that which for men is each city, this for the Pantokrator is...

before: “May the Lord bless you and keep you, may the Lord make his face shine upon you and have mercy on you, may the Lord lift up his face upon you and give you peace.” (Numbers 6:24-26). In order to show three persons, he did not say once: “the Lord bless you and shine upon you and give you peace,” but a third time he named [him] “Lord.”

And just as when a Persian prophet speaks divinely, bearing a voice from the person of the Father having such a saying: “Be strong, Zerubbabel, because I am with you; and my good word and my spirit are in your midst” (Haggai 2:4); and Isaiah, saying that his mission has become similar to the similar ones of the self-existent hypostases, and in a few words indicating all their communion, cries out: “And now the Lord, the Lord has sent me and his spirit” (Isaiah 48:16). For he did not simply name a second time “Lord, Lord” and thus “his spirit,” but so that he might also show the hypostases and the one divinity and will.

And David also, for he himself rises by such a heading and makes all his songs full and proclaims, in what way he had faith according to these words: in Psalm 17: “Who is a god beside the Lord, and who is a god besides our God? The God who girds me with power”; in Psalm 58: “You are my God, the one who takes hold of me. My God, his mercy himself will come to my aid. My God will show me in my enemies”; in Psalm 95: “Sing to the Lord a new song, sing to the Lord, all the earth, sing to the Lord, bless his name”; for having named a third time either Lord or God, he demonstrated the Trinity.

But also Hannah, praying toward the kingdoms, called upon the Trinity saying: “Adonai, Lord, Eloi Sabaoth” (1 Samuel 2:1). For “Adonai” is interpreted with the Hebrew voice as “Lord”; and again with the Greek voice he said “Lord.” And a third time in Hebrew he said “Eloi Sabaoth,” which is: God of hosts, or of powers. And now also Elijah...

The Thessian, in the third history of kings, having prayed to revive the son of the Sidonian widow who was dead, breathed a third time into him and thus raised him up, showing not only through this that he himself in prayer called upon the life-giving Trinity, but also teaching us to believe and glorify no other way.
And encouraging the water-bearers to 'dip twice' and 'dip thrice', he indicated that the three highly-praised hypostases work equally and similarly everywhere in all things.

And if you wish, I will once again make known to you from a divine voice that which is moving. For in the book of Genesis, at the tower, God and Father spoke the blessed hypostases toward his own Son and his own Holy Spirit, saying: 'Come, let us descend and let us pour out their tongues there, so that each might not hear the voice of his neighbor' (Genesis 11:7).

And Moses, as I think, showing the equality of the Trinity, set forth one vine in three stocks, saying that this other stock is nowhere more advanced, so that no one might think this hypostasis to precede that one, but that we all believe the three are joined in one divinity.

For this reason also the God-breathed Scripture forbade making steps at the altar, in which the Trinity is glorified, so that the divine hypostases might not be defined as being men according to some sort of gradation.

And simply the Old Testament, bearing a type of the new, discourses mystically and in anticipation, rather alluding in many things than stating in one; and stating more than alluding to the mystery revealed later, so that it might neither strike the unhearing and not yet stable and receptive of theophany with a blunt blow, nor perhaps cause complete harm; for the one was of infinity, and the other of inhumanity. And often also whatever was expressed here to us obscurely,

before: By this being corrupted, it is as if it were perishing, such as that which is called eternal losing out of itself, that is, being changed; it finds death, even if it remains otherwise, by its own alteration. For whatever you perceive to have happened later, this is the death of the former; it is like something such as evil happening, whereby goodness is killed by it, from which it departed, by the goodness; and the reverse, goodness by evil. For there is something which, though it must always stand by the first principle, even if it did not deny this to them, does not endure.

Indeed, Peter discusses these things in the epistles: 'If God did not spare the sinned angels, but cast them into Tartarus in chains of darkness, to be kept for judgment on the great day' (2 Peter 2:4), and 'he did not spare the ancient world' (2 Peter 2:5); and Jude: 'and angels who did not keep their own dominion, but left their own habitation, he has kept in chains of darkness under gloom to be judged on the great day' (Jude 1:6). And the rational material creation receives alteration: in one respect as Jude lost sanctification; and as Paul writes: 'the woman who lives in dissipation has been made dead, though she lives' (1 Timothy 5:5); even while enduring life in man. But in essence, it is as perishing first, and then falling into immortality. 'For it is necessary,' he says, 'that this corruptible put on incorruption, and this mortal put on immortality' (1 Corinthians 15:53). And the irrational creation undergoes a change and passes away: as it was foretold when light turns into darkness and water into blood: 'this is the alteration of the right hand of the Most High'; and elsewhere: 'the heaven,' he says, 'and the earth will pass away' (Matthew 24:35). For it was foretold that there would be new heavens and a new earth. For everything that received a beginning truly has also an end.

But the Holy Spirit, being of that unspeakable and all-prevailing eternal and incorruptible nature, and always having [it] in the same way and according to the same things; only as a mode and performing the things of God; and being a guardian of all, both the rational and perfecting the faith of the irrational, and of the irrational, until the condition of abiding in identity was given to the irrational; has been made unfit for a change of nature and a change of will, which is incorruptible. For the unshakeable is indeed incorruptible, and immediately it is without beginning, without end, and surpassing eternity. And the one without beginning:
self-acting God

before: They say that He, knowing only the things of God and being present over all, is such: 2.2 Moses in Genesis speaks from the face of God, saying, 'My spirit shall not remain in these men forever because they are flesh.' Haggai similarly speaks from a divine voice, 'I am with you, and my spirit has stood in your midst.' 2.3 Zechariah similarly says, 'But listen to my words, and receive my statutes, which I command by my spirit to my servants the prophets.' 2.4 Isaiah speaks of the Son from the Father, 'My spirit is upon you, and the words which I have given into your mouth shall not fail from your mouth and from the mouth of your seed'; he calls them 'seed', whom he also called to sonship. 2.5 And again from the Son, 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me.' To complete these things in the economy, Matthew said thus, 'So that what was said through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, saying: "Behold my servant whom I have loved, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased; I will put my spirit upon him."' 2.6 And again from the Father, 'For a spirit shall proceed from me.' 2.7 And in Ezekiel, the Most High Father names our spirit 'your' spirit, but names the Holy Spirit his own, since it has proceeded from him according to nature: 'And I will give you a new heart and a new spirit; and I will take the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh, and I will give my spirit in you.' 2.8 And in Joel, 'I will pour out from my spirit upon all flesh.' 2.9 And Paul wrote to Titus that these things have been accomplished: 'When the grace of our salvation appeared, not according to works which we ourselves did, but according to his great mercy, having regenerated us through the bath of rebirth and renewal of the Holy Spirit, which he poured out upon us richly through Jesus Christ.' 2.10 And when did he pour out? When Christ, breathing, was saying, 'Receive the Holy Spirit.' And also the 'poured out', since water from him proceeds similarly and divine myrrh, which will be shown to us in the fitting places at the right time. 2.11 And the 'upon all flesh.' For these words fit the shared essence of the Holy Trinity, not the unshared created rational nature; for not...

What is written does not say, 'I will pour out from the archangel,' but 'from my spirit,' and not in such a broad manner, but 'upon all flesh.' David, entreating, cries, 'Do not take your holy spirit from me' (Psalm 51:11), and again, 'Your holy spirit shall guide me in a straight path' (Psalm 139:24). Matthew says from the Son, 'It is not you who speak, but the spirit of my Father speaking in you' (Matthew 10:20), which is to say: not you the creatures, but the uncreated spirit of God.

Paul also writes to the Corinthians in the first epistle, 'What eye has not seen, and what ear has not heard, and what has not come up upon the heart of man: what God has prepared for those who love him, which God has revealed to us through his spirit. The spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For what does a man know of the things of the man, if not the spirit of the man that is in him? In the same way, no one knows the things of God, if not the spirit of God. But we have not received a spirit of the world, but the spirit which is from God, so that we may know the things granted to us by God' (1 Corinthians 2:9-12).

The 'prepared' good things from God, he said, that 'the spirit' 'revealed' as a companion; and 'his spirit' by antithesis to our own spirit. And securing again that it not be thought of as an angel or some other created spirit, he brought forward: 'we have not received a spirit of the world'—that is, a generated one—'but the spirit which is from God'—that is, from the remaining [essence], the one proceeding from the hypostasis of God; and as it alone knows the things of God, as Lord, and having likewise toward the Father according to nature. For the 'servant,' as it says in the Gospel, 'does not know what his lord does' (Luke 12:30).

No longer, however, did he speak as if regarding the man who dwells 'in God,' so that the uncomposed God might be thought of as composite. To the Ephesians: 'Do not grieve the holy spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption' (Ephesians 4:30); to the Romans: 'you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit, if the spirit of God dwells in you; but if anyone does not have the spirit of Christ, he is not his' (Romans 8:9); to the Galatians: 'because you are sons, God has sent the spirit of his son into your hearts, crying Abba Father' (Galatians 4:6); to the Philippians: 'for I know that...'

before: The ages, if not the Only-begotten? Who are those who have exchanged his glory? They are those saying, 'glory to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit,' who also glorify him as a creature and not even as an eternal king.

Then he says to the same [people], 'in order that they might be without excuse, because having known God, they did not glorify him as God or gave thanks, but were made vain in their reasonings, and their foolish heart was darkened' (2 Cor 5:21).
