before: They think that the intelligible things are made similar to the flows of matter. For the heavenly things surpass all mind and all thought, while the earthly and lowly things are subject to becoming and passing away in time. But especially, [the Son] was begotten without beginning, co-existing and co-working with his own true Father, like light to the solar disk. And the fact that God, Lord, Holy, Creator, Imperishable, Life, Light, and all that the Father is, exists, is testified from the Scriptures. And it is more fitting to have the similar and equal from the many than the dissimilar from the one. How is it that Adam and Eve, not having been begotten and not having had a father, have become equal in nature to those from them? Or what simple comparison have they made, saying the 'dissimilar,' or how, having measured, have they arrived at the 'greater and larger'? For Scripture neither defines the holy and unbegotten, one and indivisible Trinity by nature, nor again distinguishes for it the first and the second. But these two things are being made manifest: that the greater is not in any way heterousios, and that the comparative terms apply to those of the same substance, not to those of different substance. Nor would one say it is opportune even by imposition, not even concerning the 'incomparable and greater.' Not according to size or any volume; for the God Word has withdrawn from all magnitude and simplicity, and from all bulk, composition, and form, just as the Father and his Holy Spirit, being contained by nothing, yet containing all. Because he is also the beginning of all magnitudes, like a creator. For where is size in the most sublime, supersubstantial, and superior hypostases? Nor even according to the unbegotten. For he co-exists with the Father as an 'emanation of his glory' and not having God before him. For he indeed says: 'In the beginning was the Word' (John 1:1). And God the Creator is not measured by time relative to the creation. Since it is necessary for them to require—which is a dangerous thought to conceive—a time prior to the unbegotten and incomprehensible God and Father, and thus to compare. But men are accustomed to call 'greater' those who have preceded in time in generation, according to Isaac who ordains: 'the greater shall serve the less.' Nor as a cause. [Text ends abruptly]
He is not the cause of it. For the only-begotten Son was shown to be without beginning, since he is greater than both himself and us in the same way, which would be impossible to say or even to hear.

Nor [is he greater] according to essence and similarity. For from him it is said, 'as the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth' (John 1:14), and as 'the character of the hypostasis,' being a character toward all things, and as 'the image of God,' whom 'he who has seen has seen the Father' (John 14:9). 'For in him dwells all the fullness of deity' (Colossians 2:9). And this is drawn out by the testimony of 'let us make man in our image and according to our likeness' (Genesis 1:26).

Nor [is he greater] according to a distinction of quality, since the divine and unsearchable hypostases are not qualities; for quality belongs to bodies, but they are incorporeal and intellectual. But it is not even possible to think about them [in terms of comparison], as if the beautiful were more beautiful than the lovely, similarly to the voice of Paul speaking concerning another: 'But now these three remain, faith, hope, love; but the greatest of these is love' (1 Corinthians 13:13). For through the distinction toward virtue, he gained the 'greater' through love. For, he says, having loved, we believe, and having believed, we hope to reign with Christ.

For if the 'one God' (1 Corinthians 8:6) and 'that you may become partakers of the divine nature' (2 Peter 1:4) and not of natures, is true, and it has been demonstrated that the whole thing is one, I say: the deity. Nor [is he greater] according to equality, because it is written that the Son is 'God,' great and 'over all' (Ephesians 1:22), 'making himself equal to the Father' (Philippians 2:6) and 'swearing by himself, since he has no greater' (Hebrews 6:13).

Nor [is he greater] according to power. For it is written: 'the power of God and the wisdom of God' (1 Corinthians 1:24), and 'all things as the Father does, the Son also does in the same way' (John 14:10). Nor [is he greater] according to glory or any honor. 'For if we had known,' he says, 'we would not have crucified the Lord of glory' (1 Corinthians 2:8). And it is the will of the Father, according to John, 'that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father' (John 5:23).

According to what, then, remains the greater and the dissimilar? As it was shown, according to nothing. And indeed the apostle, preventing the impious suppositions of heretics regarding the only-begotten Son and God, yet [preventing] the identity of nature toward his Father, and furthermore proclaiming the without-beginning, having written as was said above: 'who being the radiance of the glory of the Father' (Hebrews 1:3) brought forth: 'and the character of his hypostasis.'

before: When the worthy must be revealed. And let Peter write, as it is foretold: the Spirit was sent from heaven; let it be understood in the same way that the Son was sent. For that word is as a word, and this both as a saying and a Spirit sent from God. And because of the knowing that things said from Christ or from the Holy Spirit are also said from the Father through the one will, such things are words. For he neither is ignorant nor is he sent as a slave, nor does he speak or do or come from himself as an opponent.

That no one sees God and Father, except the Son alone and the Holy Spirit; and toward those saying: 'It is not written, then,' he says, 'that the angels see the face of the Father?' Creation does not see God and Father in the way that He is; for this is of a different nature, incorporeal and uncontainable. And toward this is: 'No one shall see my face and live' (John 1:18). But the Scriptures say, at times to see or know the Son alone, and at times the Holy Spirit alone, the God Father, because the Trinity is in a unity of divinity, just as the Savior says according to John: 'Not that anyone has seen the Father, except He who is from God; he has seen the Father' (John 6:46).

And the Son is from God by nature generatively, and the Holy Spirit processionally; and again: 'Nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and whoever the Son shall reveal.' And as when speaking specifically about the Holy Spirit, as was foretold, Paul writes to the Corinthians, and as Isaiah prophesies: 'Spirit of wisdom and understanding, spirit of knowledge and godliness' (Isa 11:2). It is not written, then, he says, in Matthew from the Savior: 'See, do not despise one of these little ones; for I say to you, that their angels in the heavens always see the face of my Father who is in heaven?' (Matt 18:10). Yes; but they see, not as much and as what God is, but according to how much they are able to grasp. And the only-begotten and the Holy Spirit...

before: The Son is the true and free light and teaching for all; and he mystically demonstrates this to them, which they are ignorant of, through the ever-present memory of the many-fold exodus from Egypt within them. Thus, the noble Son of God testifies by his own nature to being free from above and not to have the character of a sister to the creation—for everything produced is a slave to the one who brought it into being, and the created thing is a slave to the creator—and he says to Peter: 'From whom do the kings of the earth receive taxes or customs?' (Matt 17:25). 'From their sons or from strangers?' Answering, 'From strangers,' Jesus said to him; 'therefore the sons are free. But so that we do not scandalize them, having gone into the sea, cast a hook, and the first fish that comes up, opening its mouth, you will find a coin. Taking that, give it to them instead of me and you.' (Matt 17:27). These things regarding these matters. But others still persist.

Concerning those who mythologize that the Father made the Son through the agency of creation: Blasphemously contending and mythologizing, they say that the Father made a Son most necessary to serve him regarding the rest of the creations, no longer understanding that this depends upon their own speculative reasoning—envy and sloth and other material things. For it is necessary indeed to see even these things. For if it is good to create—just as it is good and only proper and only exceptional of the divine abundant nature, so that he might also be glorified by the created—instead of having created all things through himself, did he perhaps feel pity in some way? And if indeed it is great for those being created to be carried along by the greater—if, according to them, the Father is greater than his own Son the Word—would he have been flattered by those glorifying his making through another? And if indeed they have not fled from all things at once, both pride and weakness, in making the produced through a mediator—the one making it through himself being greater in glory than the one making it through another—for he is not yet obeying the ever-existing by the rains, and as long as he is not yet permeated, he receives fitting measures and does not have in him anything lacking; not only is the proud one proud, but if he were already shown all that he would have authority and from...

And Jesus says to Lazarus, having died, 'Come out.' And to another, 'Your sins are forgiven you'; and to another, 'I command you. Come out of it.' But the fact that God does these things through another, according to the understanding of those men, demonstrates the God the Father, for whom the lawful Paul, having been inspired by the divine Spirit, guarantees to the believers among the creators of gods.

Furthermore, he also calls 'atheists' those who before this knew only God and the Father, being outside of the Son, because he does not complete [the work] in works, writing in one way that 'you remember that once you were among the Gentiles in the flesh, those called uncircumcised by the so-called circumcision in the flesh of human making, because at that time you were without Christ, being alienated from the hope of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and being atheists in the world' (Romans 1:26-28). And in another way, 'but at that time, not knowing God, you served gods which are not gods by nature—but now, having known God, rather having been known by God, how do you turn back again to the weak and poor elements, to which you desire again to serve from above?' (Galatians 4:8-9).

But truly, the message concerning Christ and the Holy Spirit is an ever-new salvation of the elder law, not declining into old age, and the ecclesiastical institution leads more forward because of its perfection and because it has neither lawlessness troubling it nor [is it] less or greater. For he writes by word or manner with this matter, having written that 'I became [so]... pursuing the church with zeal, having become blameless according to righteousness in the law; but whatever things were gains to me, these I have counted loss for the sake of Christ. But indeed I also consider all things loss because of the surpassingness of the knowledge of Jesus Christ our Lord, for whom all things were lost to me, and I count them as rubbish, so that I may gain Christ' (Philippians 3:6-8).

To the Romans: 'For if he who comes preaches another Jesus, whom we did not preach, or if you receive a different spirit, which you did not receive' (2 Corinthians 11:4). So then, for what purpose, having given up and having thought in such a way, has he again written his own words of sharp divine knowledge? To the Corinthians, the second [time], that if anyone is reconciled to the Son, he has been reconciled to God, and that in Christ there is a covenant with the world; and it has: 'as if God were in Christ'...

(Matt 17:25). 'From their sons or from strangers?' Answering, 'From strangers,' Jesus said to him; 'therefore the sons are free. But so that we do not scandalize them, having gone into the sea, cast a hook, and the first fish that comes up, opening its mouth, you will find a coin. Taking that, give it to them instead of me and you.' (Matt 17:27). These things regarding these matters. But others still persist.

Concerning those who mythologize that the Father made the Son through the agency of creation: Blasphemously contending and mythologizing, they say that the Father made a Son most necessary to serve him regarding the rest of the creations, no longer understanding that this depends upon their own speculative reasoning—envy and sloth and other material things. For it is necessary indeed to see even these things. For if it is good to create—just as it is good and only proper and only exceptional of the divine abundant nature, so that he might also be glorified by the created—instead of having created all things through himself, did he perhaps feel pity in some way? And if indeed it is great for those being created to be carried along by the greater—if, according to them, the Father is greater than his own Son the Word—would he have been flattered by those glorifying his making through another? And if indeed they have not fled from all things at once, both pride and weakness, in making the produced through a mediator—the one making it through himself being greater in glory than the one making it through another—for he is not yet obeying the ever-existing by the rains, and as long as he is not yet permeated, he receives fitting measures and does not have in him anything lacking; not only is the proud one proud, but if he were already shown all that he would have authority and from...

And Jesus says to Lazarus, having died, 'Come out.' And to another, 'Your sins are forgiven you'; and to another, 'I command you. Come out of it.' But the fact that God does these things through another, according to the understanding of those men, demonstrates the God the Father, for whom the lawful Paul, having been inspired by the divine Spirit, guarantees to the believers among the creators of gods.

Furthermore, he also calls 'atheists' those who before this knew only God and the Father, being outside of the Son, because he does not complete [the work] in works, writing in one way that 'you remember that once you were among the Gentiles in the flesh, those called uncircumcised by the so-called circumcision in the flesh of human making, because at that time you were without Christ, being alienated from the hope of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and being atheists in the world' (Ephesians 2:12). And in another way, 'but at that time, not knowing God, you served gods which are not gods by nature—but now, having known God, rather having been known by God, how do you turn back again to the weak and poor elements, to which you desire again to serve from above?' (Galatians 4:8-9).

But truly, the message concerning Christ and the Holy Spirit is an ever-new salvation of the elder law, not declining into old age, and the ecclesiastical institution leads more forward because of its perfection and because it has neither lawlessness troubling it nor [is it] less or greater. For he writes by word or manner with this matter, having written that 'I became [so]... pursuing the church with zeal, having become blameless according to righteousness in the law; but whatever things were gains to me, these I have counted loss for the sake of Christ. But indeed I also consider all things loss because of the surpassingness of the knowledge of Jesus Christ our Lord, for whom all things were lost to me, and I count them as rubbish, so that I may gain Christ' (Philippians 3:6-8).

To the Romans: 'For if he who comes preaches another Jesus, whom we did not preach, or if you receive a different spirit, which you did not receive' (2 Corinthians 11:4). So then, for what purpose, having given up and having thought in such a way, has he again written his own words of sharp divine knowledge? To the Corinthians, the second [time], that if anyone is reconciled to the Son, he has been reconciled to God, and that in Christ there is a covenant with the world; and it has: 'as if God were in Christ'...

before: The divine energy does not manifest itself in such a way as a life-giving spirit, which is God's inherent substance that gives life to all things, according to Paul, the trumpet of faith, writing to the Romans: 'for the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death' (Romans 8:2); and again: 'he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his indwelling Spirit in you' (Romans 8:11); and to the Corinthians: 'not that we are sufficient to consider anything as being from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God, who has made us ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter, but of the spirit. For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life' (2 Corinthians 3:6). By 'letter' he said the Mosaic law, which forbids: 'eye for an eye and tooth for a tooth' (Exodus 21:24) and defends against the lawless living; but the Holy Spirit of God is life-giving, having made us no longer under law, but under grace, and having guaranteed not to fail, to give 'evil for evil,' but rather good for evil. 'If,' he says, 'your enemy hungers, feed him'; and again to the same: 'the first Adam became a living soul, the last Adam a life-giving spirit' (1 Corinthians 15:45); and to the Galatians: 'he who sows into the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life' (Galatians 6:8); and according to John, saying from the Savior: 'it is the Spirit that gives life' (John 6:63). Ezekiel himself declares this very thing, and prophesies that with God, as His Spirit, He will perform the resurrection: 'thus says the Lord to these dry bones: behold, I am bringing into you a spirit of life, and I will cause nerves to come upon you, and I will cause flesh to rise upon you, and I will stretch skin over you, and I will give my Spirit upon you, and you shall live and you shall know that I am the Lord' (Ezekiel 37:12-14). Therefore, the essential life and the life-giving power has neither beginning nor end nor alteration; and do not let this fall to these by nature and truth of God.

For which is it, even as those things which are apart from the God and Father are possessed by inheritance. For no created thing can be a cause of life or show life in itself; but all things deprived of the divine Spirit are dead; 'for in him we live and move and are,' as the apostolic acts said (Acts 17:28). And indeed, if all things that come into being and are perishable, and those things which are perishing, remain without life: how could he grant these things to others, of which he himself becomes lacking? We are therefore made alive by the Holy Spirit, just as by him who said: 'I am the resurrection and the life' (John 11:25).

It has been written that because of the identity of divinity and the equal energy, as he raised Christ, who suffered in the flesh through us, sometimes the Father, sometimes himself, sometimes the Holy Spirit. And according to the heretical exposition: that because of the identity of divinity and the one energy, the scriptures say, as he raised Jesus Christ according to the form of a servant, sometimes the Father, sometimes himself, sometimes the Holy Spirit; but the actions are not so: 'God raised this one on the third day' (Acts 2:24), as John says from the Savior: 'destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. But he was speaking about the temple of his own body' (John 2:19-21); and again: 'I lay down my soul, so that I may take it again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it again' (John 10:17-18). Peter in the first epistle says: 'Christ died once for sins on our behalf, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might bring us to God; having been put to death in the flesh, but having been made alive in the spirit' (1 Peter 3:18).

That he creates and raises from the dead. In the same way, that he who created is to sanctify is more necessary than the creating. And according to the heretical exposition: that the great creation creates man and raises from the dead and makes alive and returns to heaven and renewed the earth which had been corrupted by human lawlessness.

before: Unbegotten life is the substance of the generated nature of men.

15.20 The saying, 'and the light shines in the darkness and the darkness did not overcome it' (John 1:5), does not admit the opinions of the heretics. For it declares both secretly and very sharply—as if anyone had perceived a prior time or an untimely moment or an eternal age—that it shines eternally as an inseparable radiance of God, and never did the darkness of non-existence overcome it.
15.21 The 'Almighty' (Rev 1:8) requires no interpretation. For it shows that he has an undivided kingdom toward God the Father and His Holy Spirit, and that he is 'God over all' (Ps 86:8).
15.22 The 'one coming' (2 Thess 2:8) signifies the Son who is about to come a second time and 'to judge the living and the dead' (Acts 10:42).

15.23 Thus the Baptist John also establishes that since 'the One Who Is' (Exod 3:14) is said concerning the Son, he declares to the Lord: 'You are' instead of 'that one who is', whom I myself, being in the desert of the wilderness and through the fluttering, having recognized as being in the Virgin the God, worshipped, 'or are we waiting for another?'.

15.24 And in the first epistle, John the friend and apostle of the Lord writes: 'That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life—and the life was manifested, and we have seen and testify and announce to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was manifested to us—that which we have seen and heard, we announce to you also, so that you also may have fellowship with us. And our fellowship is with the Father and with His Son Jesus Christ' (1 John 1:1-3).

15.25 Attend again to the multitude of the 'was', and how those not confessing according to nature that he is the Son co-ruling with God do not have the fellowship of salvation with the Father or the Only-Begotten.

15.26 For toward this faith delivered to us in the mystagogy of the illumination by the Lord of all is the fellowship which Peter wrote: 'that you might become partakers of the divine nature' (2 Pet 1:4). For the creature, being under time, is not a divine nature.
15.27 And remember in these things that since he said 'our fellowship' 'with the Father and with His Son', he spoke in equal terms, and not 'through His Son'.
15.28 And Amos

And the prophet, prophesying 'Pantokrator', names the Son similarly, saying: 'He who builds up his ascent into heaven and lays the foundation of his promise upon the earth, the one calling the water of the sea and pouring it upon the face of all the earth, Lord, God, Pantokrator, let that be his name.'

David also sings concerning an ascent: 'God has ascended in shouts of joy, the Lord in the sound of a trumpet' (Ps 47:5). Both these things are about the Son. For the Father neither descended nor ascended, as the apostle interprets, writing thus: 'And what is this "ascended", if not that he also descended first? He is the one who descended and the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things,' as he says that, having ascended above all, he is also carrying [all things] above, together with the Father who begot him, who is unbegotten.

For this is manifest to one having understood, from which even the noetic powers differ, since they are found to be measured creatures in heaven, but not above the heavens, nor are they able to fill all things. And Wisdom similarly proclaims him 'Pantokrator', saying: 'This [will act] against them instead of their insolence, because they mocked and magnified themselves against the Lord the Pantokrator. The Lord will appear upon them, and the Lord will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth, and each will prostrate himself from his place' (Wisdom).

And Malachi likewise speaks from the face of the Master: 'For from the rising of the sun and to its setting my name shall be glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name and a pure sacrifice. For great is my name among the nations, says the Lord Pantokrator. But you profane it' (Mal 1:11). For the memory of both the appearance and of being glorified among the nations shows the Son, whose name the Jews profane along with the worshipers of creatures. And this very sequence intends for him to be Pantokrator, since he is the icon and the only-begotten, having been endowed with Pantokrator, and in this also he is to be understood as the icon of the Pantokrator.

And Paul writes to the Hebrews: 'Who, being the radiance of the glory of the Father' (Heb 1:3), that is, co-ruler and consubstantial. For so that the incomparable might be shown somewhat through a parable, even if thus much it might be received into the mind, which is above the mind,

before: 21. Concerning speaking of the Trinity among the faithful, because of the unchangeable nature and essence. And speaking equally of the divine hypostases among the saints proclaims the unchangeability of nature and authority. For Zechariah—not the prophet, but the father of John—said that the Lord God of Israel has spoken through the prophets (Luke 1:68). And Paul similarly sent to the Hebrews: 'God, having spoken many times and in many ways of old to the fathers in the prophets, has spoken to us in this last age in His Son' (Hebrews 1:1-2). And to the Corinthians he wrote concerning the Son: 'since you seek the testing of the Christ speaking in me' (2 Corinthians 13:3). And the Savior according to Matthew teaches: 'for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father is the one speaking in you' (Matthew 10:20).

22. Concerning the fact that it is written that we live by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit through the same Word, which is the consubstantiality of the Trinity. What is written—that we live by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—teaches this to be seen most clearly; just as when Paul reasons with the Romans in letters: 'you consider yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord' (Romans 6:11). And again: 'that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for Him, Christ, who died for them and was raised up' (2 Corinthians 5:15); and to the Galatians: 'if we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit' (Galatians 5:25).

23. Concerning the fact that through this Word, the law from above is written to be of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Because of whom we said it is the Word, and the law from above is written to be of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, just as the Psalmist says in Psalm 40: 'the law of his God is in his heart,' and in Psalm 39: 'to do your will, O God, I have desired, and your law is in the midst of my womb' (Psalm 40:8; 39:8). And as Paul writes to the Galatians: 'Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ' (Galatians 6:2).

And to the Corinthians in the first epistle: “To those without law I became as without law — not being without God’s law, but under Christ’s law — that I might win those without law” (1 Cor 9:21). And to the Romans: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death” (Rom 8:2). And again, hinting at the new and the old covenant, he says: “But now we have been discharged from the law, having died to that by which we were held, so that we serve in newness of spirit and not in oldness of letter” (Rom 7:6); and again: “For we know that the law is spiritual” (Rom 7:14).

24. Concerning our being called men of God or Christians or spiritual ones, on account of the same cause of consubstantiality in the Trinity. So then, on this account we are called either men of God or Christians or spiritual ones. For thus the widow in Zarephath says to Elijah the Tishbite: “What have you to do with me, man of God?” (1 Kings 17:18); and again: “Now I know that you are a holy man of God” (1 Kings 17:24). And the Shunammite to her husband concerning the prophet Elisha: “See, a great man of God is coming to us” (2 Kings 4:9). And the royal histories: “And a man of God came from Judah and prophesied against the altar in Bethel” (1 Kings 13:1). And the Psalmist in the inscription of the 89th Psalm: “A prayer of Moses, the man of God” (Ps 89 LXX).

And Paul, writing to Timothy a second time: “that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work” (2 Tim 3:17). And the Acts: “And it happened that they were gathered together in the church for a whole year, and the disciples were first called Christians in Antioch” (Acts 11:26). And Paul, speaking to the Corinthians in an epistle: “Now concerning spiritual things I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers. You know that when you were Gentiles you were led to the speechless idols, as you were led away. Therefore […].”

before: I will say—the great and only great thing compared by a small thing—as at once from the sun and from the nature of the sun, and from the whole disk, indivisibly and without separation and equally, the whole light is co-manifested and co-operates and co-provides heat to those receptive of sensation. And the light of the pre-existing essence, being immediately and not later poured out and co-proceeding and co-woven, manifests its quality entirely within itself.

15.36 But, regarding those [words], 'there was when there was not' the radiance, where is the radiance-emitting hypostasis of the light? For it must have certainly slid along with that. And indeed Daniel, prophesying, said: 'and light was with him' (Dan 4:35) instead of 'the Son with the Father'. 15.37 For this most demonstrates the unmixed and great nature of the divinity, that the Father begat it co-beginning and co-existing, and at once perfect and unchangeable and impassible.

before: Having been refreshed by apostolic testimony and witness, he says: 'Stephen, having been filled with the Holy Spirit, saw the heavens opened' (Acts 7:55). Thus it is as has been received from of old: from heaven, therefore, is the unapproachable, spotless ether.

He is a prophet, that is, he foreknows, just as the Father and the Son do; but it belongs to the divine nature alone to know precisely the things that are to come. For creation, while it brings forward all things that are speculative from itself, sees only unerringly and without deviation that which the Holy Spirit teaches it. For by His divine rays, it not only illuminates the powers in heaven once, but also brightens the eyes of our souls, and it frequently shows in many ways the things to come, and it facilitates through its own goodness and philanthropy those things contributing to the useful for human nature, so that one might say of creation: it is such when our sleeping nature does not write [its destiny] through the provider by means of creation, but upon itself.

And the testimonies concerning the foreknowledge of the Spirit from the apostolic deeds are in these things. From Peter to the Jews: 'Men, brothers, it was necessary for the Scripture to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas, the guide of those who seized Jesus' (Acts 1:16; 13:27). So indeed he said 'it was necessary'; for every word of God alone is not incomplete. And from Paul: 'The Holy Spirit testifies to me city by city, saying, that tribulations and distresses remain with me' (2 Cor 11:26). And through the prophet Agabus, he forewarned of a famine coming under heaven because of the failings of men, as a good thing, just as also regarding Nineveh, that if they had been made reverent by repentance they would flee the evil (Acts 11:28; Jonah 3:10), which also happened to many in later times during [the reign of] Claudius. And in the Gospel, Christ says concerning the Spirit: 'And He will announce to you the things that are coming,' that is, the things to come (John 16:13).

before: reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and having established among us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we intercede for Christ as the God entreating through us. We pray on behalf of Christ: 'be reconciled to God.'

And again, as he used to preach all other things, he cried out loudly that even what seemed difficult was made easy to Christ because of his philanthropic economy, all glory and strength overflowing, doing this by work, so that one might not overlook the unbegotten, unmixed, and unchangeable divinity of the one from the glorious passion, lest a scripture of pride should offend. And he was saying such things: 'not to judge anything in you except Jesus Christ and this one crucified' (cf. 1 Cor 2:8). And to the Romans: 'the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe' (Rom 3:22).

Each is justified by God through the faith he speaks of toward the Son. And to the Galatians: 'knowing that no man is justified by works of the law except through faith in Jesus Christ, and we believed in Jesus Christ so that we might be justified from the faith of Christ and not from works of the law, because no flesh shall be justified by works of the law' (Gal 2:16). And he explains also to others that 'neither circumcision avails nor uncircumcision, but a new faith working through love' (Gal 5:6).

Of the word deepening the mind, it is to be developed. Therefore he intends to teach that the appearance of Christ is something new and that the only faith was found for all men; according to which he leaves no place, neither in Judaism nor in Hellenism. And this could be understood also according to: 'behold, the old things have passed away, all things have become new' (Rev 21:5). And so that it may be understood, he who knows God ceases to say that the circumcision is not perfect.

And the Son took up into salvation and teaching for all the true and free light; and he presents this to some of them as being mystically unknown through the inward memory of the exodus from Egypt. Therefore, the venerable Son of God bears witness to his own nature to the freedom from above, and not as a sister having the creation—for everything produced is a slave to the one who brought it into being, and the created thing is a slave to the one who created it.

He says to Peter: 'From whom do the kings of the earth receive taxes or custom? From their own sons or from others?' Answering: 'From others,' Jesus said to him, 'so then the sons are free. In order that we might not scandalize them, having gone into the sea, cast a hook and the first fish coming up, Peter, and having opened its mouth, you will find a stater. Taking that, give it to them instead of me and you.' (Matt 22:16-22). These things indeed concerning these. But they still do not cease.

Concerning those mythologizing that the Father made the Son by the ministry of creation. 8.1 Dealing blasphemously and mythologizing, they say that the Father made a Son most necessary to minister to Him regarding the rest of the creatures, no longer understanding how this depended on this speculative word of theirs: envy and sloth and other material things. 8.2 For it is necessary indeed even to see these things. For if it is good to create—just as it is good and only proper and only exceptional of the divine abundant nature, so that he might also be glorified by the one [who receives it]—instead of having created all things through Himself, did He somewhat grow weary? 8.3 And if indeed it is great for those being created to be carried along by the greater, if according to them the Father is greater than His own Son the Word, did He court those glorifying Him for His making through another? 8.4 And if indeed they have not fled from all things at once, both pride and weakness, the making of the proceeding through a mediator makes the one doing it through Himself appear greater in glory than the one doing it through another. 8.5 For not being the ever-existing, He obeys the waves, and as long as He is not yet passing through, He receives the fitting measures and does not have in Him anything lacking; not only is the proud one proud, but he would already be shown to be lacking in all things and in authority. And when Jesus says to Lazarus, having died, 'Come out' (John 11:43), and to another, 'Your sins are forgiven you' (Mark 2:5), and to another, 'I command you, come out of him'—the fact that God does these things through another, according to their mind, shows the God the Father, whose thoughts are your workings, is not able to pass through all things by Himself without the help of the one through whom or in whom He acts.

before: The master, having handed over, says: 'baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' (Matt 28:19), because of the equal, equally-powerful, and consubstantial nature and the clarity of the hypostases. When what is now said concerning God and Father is remembered differently concerning the Only-begotten or the Holy Spirit, it is because of the reasons previously stated. When the hypostases teach differently that the same works perform the same energy, it is because of what is said before. When God and Father has pleased, each hypostasis being able to create and do all things, to sustain all things through the Son and God, and to sanctify through the Holy Spirit, it is because of the single will of the Trinity and the showing that all beautiful things are supplied from it, and because it sends to us thanksgiving and doxology common and equal to itself. When the same names are used for the blessed Trinity, such as 'God', 'Lord', 'Holy', 'Just', 'Good' and such things—except that 'the Father' is alone and always Father, and 'the true Son and God' is the Son and God without beginning, and 'the Holy Spirit' is the one and the same Spirit of God without beginning—it is because of the communion of nature, kingship, and all things. This, however, is upon it alone: when they discourse in secret, because the mystery of the faith is always kept to be revealed only to the faithful. When they say the Father God begat, the Son the Word being begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeding, it is because of the divine thinking from the hypostasis of the Father as being without beginning and without passion, and having already preceded and being unified, not as near to creatures.

When he says, 'the Father who sent me is greater than I' (John 14:28) and whatever has been thought to be small regarding divinity, it is because of his inexpressible and voluntary economy for our sake and on behalf of you. For upon divinity, neither the small nor the non-omnipresent has place. When the Son says, 'My Father has given me a commandment, what shall I say and what shall I speak, and from myself I have not spoken' (John 14:10), and concerning the Holy Spirit, 'he will not speak from himself' (John 16:13) and such things, it is because of the harmony of the divine hypostases and because the teachings and gifts of the blessed Trinity are common and not different...

Those striving to be a temple, however worthy of the Holy Spirit dwelling in the faithful, as having once received the inaccessible light shining in them, glorify equally—as the Master established in the mystery of baptism—the self-generated God and Father, and the beloved and only-begotten Word Son co-existing with Him, and the mentioned Holy Spirit proceeding from His only hypostasis unoriginally and without distinction.

They do not disbelieve in the consubstantiality of the Trinity, nor do they seek a way or difference of generation and procession; because even regarding the heavenly liturgical powers, He has established this as unknown, inexpressible, and fearsome to remember; and how the Holy Trinity, having itself existed unoriginally, always possesses likewise and in such ways; and how, being seated upon the eternal throne, it looks upon the abysses, and while silencing, hears, and while hearing, remains silent; and knowing the future before the actual; and by word, and even more than word, by the mere will to lead all things; and before one scratches in the heart, it immediately provides the vote upon the request; and it accords all things at all times for benefit; and to be slow for wrath, but ready for goodness; and to be angry through our deficiency, but to remit the punishment through its own philanthropy.

And moreover, it is still incomprehensible how it has one will, and speaks, and provides common things of itself; and it overshadows not so much for the well-being of bodies, but the crushed heart itself. And indeed also this, how it exists invisible and ungraspable by seraphic eyes, uncontainable by word and place, undivided in power, unsearchable, immeasurable, simple, and unyielding; all-seeing, all-hearing, and the hope of all; far more luminous than heavenly light, and higher than all height, as much as cannot be said, and more intellectual by an infinite word than every mind.

For how could the things of the Trinity not be incomprehensible to all, when it is the creator of all and higher than all noetic, and even more so than noetic creation, beyond which is absolutely nothing, and all things...

before: "Creator" and "Ruler" and "His peace has no limit" and "Savior" and "Christ is all in all" and "Blessed forever," and that "great is the mystery of godliness," are clear; for among the Christians, Christ is praised as an unbegotten God, and that by his own divinity "he acquires the people," because he has consubstantiality with the Father.

Thus, the saints who are now to be remembered by us speak concerning these things, to whom God, according to Psalm 19, "made known the ways of life." David, in Psalm 67, prays: "Arise, O Lord my God, by command, which I have decreed, and let a gathering of peoples surround you, and return to the heights on account of this."

One perceives, as the prophet sees, that he knows the Lord and God, and he petitions him, saying "Arise" upon your unutterable becoming-human, in the manner which you foretold: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19).

For on account of this, they say, of which salvation is surrounding us: "The nations shall surround you by faith; and you, from whence you came, shall return unseparatedly"; and in Psalm 45: "Great God, Lord, and great King over all the earth." And in Psalm 44: "From the risings of the sun even to the settings, the splendor of his beauty is from Zion; God shall come visibly"; and in Psalm 67: "Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered," and "Make way for him who has set foot toward the west; Lord is his name"; and in Psalm 69: "Arise, O God, judge the earth."

Behold, how each word lifts up the glory concerning him and suffices to persuade that he exists as the essence of the Father's unity; and that the great writer calls God he who was placed in the tomb not without life, so that he might save both the living and those departed from human affairs, and he prophesies rising, judging those who have thought wisely regarding so much and such a great blessing.
Know, however, that "the west" refers to the last times; for in them this spectacle has visibly appeared to this world.

And in Psalm 69: "In the holy is your way. Who is a great God like our God? You are the God who does wonders alone." Here the incarnate God-Word is praised without words, he who entered into the Jewish temple and taught and worked wonders.

Regarding the root: 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; great God, Lord, and appeared to us' (Ps 2:2). 27.12 If it is logical according to the prophet that the Lord who appeared to us is 'great God' and 'blessed' (that is, glorified), and also 'great King' and 'only wonder-worker,' and is the Son—it is not logical according to the heretics to imply he is lesser than his own Father. 27.13 For it is not possible for the same [person] to possess [these things] first according to the prophecy, and second according to them.

27.14 If indeed we ask of the same Psalmist, we shall learn that just as the Father is known, so also the Son exists as the God of the forefathers. 27.15 For in the 44th Psalm he has cried out: 'God has reigned over the nations. God sits upon His holy throne; rulers of peoples have been gathered with the God of Abraham' (Ps 47:8). 27.16 But they were gathered together with the God who became man, concerning whom it is sung in the 2nd Psalm: 'Why did the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? after: "Creator" and "Ruler" and "His peace has no limit" and "Savior" and "Christ is all in all" and "Blessed forever," and that "great is the mystery of godliness," are clear; for among the Christians, Christ is praised as an unbegotten God, and that by his own divinity "he acquires the people," because he has consubstantiality with the Father.

David, in Psalm 67, prays: "Arise, O Lord my God, by command, which I have decreed, and let a gathering of peoples surround you, and return to the heights on account of this."

One perceives, as the prophet sees, that he knows the Lord and God, and he petitions him, saying "Arise" upon your unutterable becoming-human, in the manner which you foretold: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (John 2:19).

For on account of this, they say, of which salvation is surrounding us: "The nations shall surround you by faith; and you, from whence you came, shall return unseparatedly"; and in Psalm 45: "Great God, Lord, and great King over all the earth." And in Psalm 44: "From the risings of the sun even to the settings, the splendor of his beauty is from Zion; God shall come visibly"; and in Psalm 67: "Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered," and "Make way for him who has set foot toward the west; Lord is his name"; and in Psalm 69: "Arise, O God, judge the earth."

Behold, how each word lifts up the glory concerning him and suffices to persuade that he exists as the essence of the Father's unity; and that the great writer calls God he who was placed in the tomb not without life, so that he might save both the living and those departed from human affairs, and he prophesies rising, judging those who have thought wisely regarding so much and such a great blessing.
Know, however, that "the west" refers to the last times; for in them this spectacle has visibly appeared to this world.

before: The meeting with the Lord was thought of generally—that is, with Abraham—the Melchizedek. What then is the will of their empty-headedness and how is it absurd? For they say whoever wishes to call [Him] the Beginning, and confess the end, and promise to the generation, and accept death from this [generation]; and they suppose that which comes from non-existence or from the dissimilarity of the divine essence to have become mortal and at the same time foreign to the composition of the Father, which is merely said, not even honored, as a mediator of all ungodliness.

But are their things then strong against the 'In the beginning was the Word' (John 1:1)? It was written also concerning creation, he says, the 'was'. For it has 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth, and the earth was formless and void' (Gen 1:1-2), and 'there was a man of Ramathaim-Ziphah' (1 Samuel 1:1). There is nothing common to the 'In the beginning was' and the 'In the beginning God made', nor to the creator in relation to the creation. For the 'was' concerning the creation is said and believed only regarding the flowing and passing time.

For the creation was after the non-existent came to be. For he said in advance that He made it, and then he added the 'was', so that it might not be thought automatic. But concerning the God the Word, it signifies the super-beginning. For 'In the beginning', he says, 'was' and 'was God' (John 1:1), and the 'In the beginning was' pushes out from non-existence.

But they testify concerning the being of the Son as eternal and maker of the ages thus: Paul, writing to the Hebrews: 'Long ago God, speaking in many parts and many ways, to the fathers by the prophets, in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages' (Heb 1:1-2); so he inherits his own things both as maker of them and as true Son; and he was appointed heir as having become man. And to the Corinthians in the first epistle: 'For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ' (1 Cor 3:11), that is, it is impossible for a beginning of the Son to be devised. 'For in him and through him' is every beginning.
And David in the 84th psalm, singing about the ruler: 'Our God, the eternal King, worked salvation in the midst of the earth' (Psalm 74:12). And he says the Golgotha, the middle place and such like.

A center which names him under heaven; in whom, by his divine foreknowledge, the Son worked out salvation for us through the incarnation, and in fact, when the impassible one suffered through goodness as he knew and willed for our sake, and reached, as they say, 'to the heart of the earth' (Ezekiel 28:26: 'I have set her, Jerusalem, in the midst of the nations'). And in the 119th Psalm: 'Forever, Lord, your word remains in heaven' (Psalm 119:89). And the Lord himself, utterly excluding the heretics, said concerning himself: 'Amen, amen, I say to you, before the ages were, I am' (John 8:58).

Regarding the establishing of all things as creator, both incorporeal and corporeal, but not as subordinate or mediator, and in this also as without beginning, according to the testimonies already set forth; and David in the 33rd Psalm sings: 'Our God in heaven and on earth did all that he willed' (Psalm 33:6). He did not say: 'all that was permitted.'

Who then would deny that the self-determining and all-determining Monad exists, the one who acts by his own will and has all things rushing together by his pure, intrinsic breath, without necessity? And in the 89th Psalm: 'You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain. And all of them will grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail' (Psalm 102:25), instead of 'you are without beginning and without end.'

And Paul writes the same to the Ephesians: 'in God who created all things' (Ephesians 3:9), and to the Colossians: 'because in him all things were created, those in the heavens and those on the earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and for him, and he is before all things, and in him all things consist' (Colossians 1:16-17). For he who essentially depicts God and the one before all things in divinity, no one surpasses or is elder than him, just as no one is subject to or later than the one who is after all things.
And in another way: if he is before all things, alone from alone and by alone, absolutely generated before every activity, and is essentially the Son of the Father. For it is necessary...

And again, as he used to preach all other things, he cried out loudly that even what seemed difficult was made easy to Christ because of his philanthropic economy, all glory and strength overflowing, doing this by work, so that one might not overlook the unbegotten, unmixed, and unchangeable divinity of the one from the glorious passion, lest a scripture of pride should offend. And he was saying such things: 'not to judge anything in you except Jesus Christ and this one crucified' (cf. 1 Corinthians 2:2). And to the Romans: 'the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe' (Rom 3:22).

Each is justified by God through the faith he speaks of toward the Son. And to the Galatians: 'knowing that no man is justified by works of the law except through faith in Jesus Christ, and we believed in Jesus Christ so that we might be justified from the faith of Christ and not from works of the law, because no flesh shall be justified by works of the law' (Gal 2:16). And he explains also to others that 'neither circumcision avails nor uncircumcision, but a new faith working through love' (Gal 5:6).

Of the word deepening the mind, it is to be developed. Therefore he intends to teach that the appearance of Christ is something new and that the only faith was found for all men; according to which he leaves no place, neither in Judaism nor in Hellenism. And this could be understood also according to: 'behold, the old things have passed away, all things have become new' (Rev 21:5). And so that it may be understood, he who knows God ceases to say that the circumcision is not perfect.

And the Son took up into salvation and teaching for all the true and free light; and he presents this to some of them as being mystically unknown through the inward memory of the exodus from Egypt. Therefore, the venerable Son of God bears witness to his own nature to the freedom from above, and not as a sister having the creation—for everything produced is a slave to the one who brought it into being, and the created thing is a slave to the one who created it.

He says to Peter: 'From whom do the kings of the earth receive taxes or custom? From their own sons or from others?' Answering: 'From others,' Jesus said to him, 'so then the sons are free. In order that we might not scandalize them, having gone into the sea, cast a hook and the first fish coming up, Peter, and having opened its mouth, you will find a stater. Taking that, give it to them instead of me and you.' (Matt 22:16-22). These things indeed concerning these. But they still do not cease.

Concerning those mythologizing that the Father made the Son by the ministry of creation. 8.1 Dealing blasphemously and mythologizing, they say that the Father made a Son most necessary to minister to Him regarding the rest of the creatures, no longer understanding how this depended on this speculative word of theirs: envy and sloth and other material things. 8.2 For it is necessary indeed even to see these things. For if it is good to create—just as it is good and only proper and only exceptional of the divine abundant nature, so that he might also be glorified by the one [who receives it]—instead of having created all things through Himself, did He somewhat grow weary? 8.3 And if indeed it is great for those being created to be carried along by the greater, if according to them the Father is greater than His own Son the Word, did He court those glorifying Him for His making through another? 8.4 And if indeed they have not fled from all things at once, both pride and weakness, the making of the proceeding through a mediator makes the one doing it through Himself appear greater in glory than the one doing it through another. 8.5 For not being the ever-existing, He obeys the waves, and as long as He is not yet passing through, He receives the fitting measures and does not have in Him anything lacking; not only is the proud one proud, but he would already be shown to be lacking in all things and in authority. And when Jesus says to Lazarus, having died, 'Come out' (John 11:43), and to another, 'Your sins are forgiven you' (Mark 2:5), and to another, 'I command you, come out of him'—the fact that God does these things through another, according to their mind, shows the God the Father, whose thoughts are your workings, is not able to pass through all things by Himself without the help of the one through whom or in whom He acts.

before: Lord: 'you alone are most high over all the earth' (Psalm 83:18), saying 'alone' because of the one divinity. He called him Father of eternity, being the creator of even the past ages, because he was known by men much more through the temporal aspect of the economy.

Therefore, he called him Father, as a creator and not of uncreated nature; for one is the Father of the uncreated and consubstantial Son. And to demonstrate his divinity, he said something simple: 'there is no limit to his peace.'

And Jeremiah, or rather, for the book of Baruch is one of both, solemnly speaks about him: 'This is our God; no other shall be reckoned against him (Isaiah 42:8). He found every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his child and to Israel, the one beloved by him; after these things he appeared upon the earth and walked among men.'

If, therefore, it is not conceived in a God-befitting manner that the present scripture was spoken thus because of the shared divinity of both the unutterable hypostases, it remains to say, effectively blaspheming, that the one who created is God and Father, but not our God, and is not comparable to his Son.

Thus, the word of those who slander has fallen away and spread, making the God the Word smaller and a subordinate. For how could another be incomparable to God, 'to whom no other shall be reckoned against him'?

And again: 'gods, who did not make heaven and earth, destroyed upon the earth; Lord, who made the heavens in wisdom, he is the living and true God' (Jeremiah 10:11), as if there were another divinity that is not true, except that of the genuine Son of God, through whom and from whom and by whom the heavens were also provided for the whole world.

And Paul, the preeminent of men, following the same sequence, gives words fittingly concerning him, writing to Titus: 'awaiting the blessed hope and the appearance of the glory of the great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, to redeem us from all lawlessness and to cleanse for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works' (Titus 2:13).

For through the being called 'the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ,' it is made manifest that he does not have a second-rank status in essence, and [the distinction] of the unoriginate toward the great God the Father.

For according to appearances it is possible to conclude that if the Son is small, how will the Father be great? If the Word God 'was when he was not' (John 1:1), he was when the name of the Father did not exist. Let it be gracious to us that we dare to say such things because of the ignorance of others. 'For piety is a beautiful habit', they say, 'for those using it'.

But through the saying 'of the one giving himself for us, in order that he might cleanse for himself a people of his own possession' (Titus 2:14)—not for another in order that he might cleanse a people—it follows what has been mentioned. For it signifies that he himself, the one single, self-possessing and good deity, who is the cause of all, has been determined. For it is a peculiar thing for a creator, indeed, not to surpass his own creation, if it must be said so of his own work; but for the deity of a beloved Son, having no difference from the Father, to acquire the people for himself.

And this great and true interpreter leads the argument to demonstrate that he is at once a philanthropic Savior God, and at once, as he himself veiled himself and did not show himself as superior in deity, to become with us as one of us, through a change and through sin, he asserts: 'When indeed the kindness and the philanthropy of our Savior God appeared, not because of the works which we ourselves did, but according to his great mercy, he saved us through the bath of regeneration and the renewal of the Holy Spirit'.

And he also reproaches the Colossians and makes a disparagement of the primary theology concerning him by the writings, as it has already been said in the chapter 'on the consubstantial': 'Why according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ Jesus? For in him dwells all the fullness of deity bodily' (Colossians 2:9), that is, essentially. For he also is by nature a fullness, the Father's deity existing in essence.

For 'being equal to God was not considered a robbery' (Philippians 2:6); but we received from the fullness because of his goodness. Which we by nature as slaves did not have, John saying: 'And from his fullness we all have received, and grace for grace' (John 1:16), that is, the grace of the rebirth instead of the grace which we were cast away from, striking at the first law given upon the single stock. 'For no longer,'
after: Lord: 'you alone are most high over all the earth' (Psalm 83:18), saying 'alone' because of the one divinity. He called him Father of eternity, being the creator of even the past ages, because he was known by men much more through the temporal aspect of the economy.

Therefore, he called him Father, as a creator and not of uncreated nature; for one is the Father of the uncreated and consubstantial Son. And to demonstrate his divinity, he said something simple: 'there is no limit to his peace.'

And Jeremiah, or rather, for the book of Baruch is one of both, solemnly speaks about him: 'This is our God; no other shall be reckoned against him (Baruch 3:35). He found every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his child and to Israel, the one beloved by him; after these things he appeared upon the earth and walked among men.'

If, therefore, it is not conceived in a God-befitting manner that the present scripture was spoken thus because of the shared divinity of both the unutterable hypostases, it remains to say, effectively blaspheming, that the one who created is God and Father, but not our God, and is not comparable to his Son.

Thus, the word of those who slander has fallen away and spread, making the God the Word smaller and a subordinate. For how could another be incomparable to God, 'to whom no other shall be reckoned against him'?

And again: 'gods, who did not make heaven and earth, destroyed upon the earth; Lord, who made the heavens in wisdom, he is the living and true God' (Jeremiah 10:11), as if there were another divinity that is not true, except that of the genuine Son of God, through whom and from whom and by whom the heavens were also provided for the whole world.

And Paul, the preeminent of men, following the same sequence, gives words fittingly concerning him, writing to Titus: 'awaiting the blessed hope and the appearance of the glory of the great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, to redeem us from all lawlessness and to cleanse for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works' (Titus 2:13).

For through the being called 'the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ,' it is made manifest that he does not have a second-rank status in essence, and [the distinction] of the unoriginate toward the great God the Father.

For according to appearances it is possible to conclude that if the Son is small, how will the Father be great? If the Word God 'was when he was not' (John 1:1), he was when the name of the Father did not exist. Let it be gracious to us that we dare to say such things because of the ignorance of others. 'For piety is a beautiful habit', they say, 'for those using it'.

But through the saying 'of the one giving himself for us, in order that he might cleanse for himself a people of his own possession' (Titus 2:14)—not for another in order that he might cleanse a people—it follows what has been mentioned. For it signifies that he himself, the one single, self-possessing and good deity, who is the cause of all, has been determined. For it is a peculiar thing for a creator, indeed, not to surpass his own creation, if it must be said so of his own work; but for the deity of a beloved Son, having no difference from the Father, to acquire the people for himself.

And this great and true interpreter leads the argument to demonstrate that he is at once a philanthropic Savior God, and at once, as he himself veiled himself and did not show himself as superior in deity, to become with us as one of us, through a change and through sin, he asserts: 'When indeed the kindness and the philanthropy of our Savior God appeared, not because of the works which we ourselves did, but according to his great mercy, he saved us through the bath of regeneration and the renewal of the Holy Spirit'.

For the Trinity is not composed of something within the one divinity, nor are the spirits [called] spirits, if we do not speak of profanities, nor are men [called] gods because they are called so; for we are not in truth. If they do not realize that these things contradict: 'only the wise God' and 'alone possessing immortality,' they will not be able to be made wise by anything from the opposite of the Holy Spirit.

For these things were thus spoken by Paul, because the Word of God is the Son, and the Holy Spirit is the Spirit, and he has it inseparably according to nature, and leads into one divinity, just as it is said by those outside: 'one God from whom all things came.' Just as Paul wrote to the Romans, Galatians, and Timothy concerning the Father: 'one God' (Romans 3:30; 1 Cor 8:6), so John said concerning the Son: 'the only begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father' (John 1:18). And concerning the Holy Spirit, Paul taught the Corinthians: 'but to another the gifts of healings in the one Spirit' (1 Cor 12:9); for the oneness of the divine and the plurality of nature are His own. And just as it was written that the Son was begotten, and the witness says: 'I came forth from the Father' (John 16:28); so it was written, and the same said: 'the Spirit of truth, which proceeds from the Father' (John 15:26), meaning it issued forth.

And just as the Son, being God and Lord, is the Son of God and Lord, so the Holy Spirit, being God and Lord, is the Spirit of God and Lord. And in the way that it is written that the Son co-exists with the Father, the same way the Holy Spirit is written 'the word of God,' and 'the spirit of his mouth,' and 'the breath of the Pantokrator' (Job 33:4), because having been co-substanced, he shone forth from him; so that no one might suppose that it is something from the outside of the divinity of the Father or of his Word. For the word of the Word and the word of the mind are His own; and this is fulfilled: 'the one God and Father of all, and over all, and through all, and in all' (Eph 4:6).

And just as the Son is shown to be distinct from the Father, as it is written: 'he who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9); likewise also the Holy Spirit, through which it is said: 'in this we know that God is in us, from his Spirit, which he gave us' (1 John 4:13). It is therefore necessary, since the true God is the Father, that a true God be equal to him and—

Indeed, John, establishing that He is in glory and that glory is owed to Him from all, said: 'And yet, despite so many signs performed by Jesus, the Jews did not believe in Him, so that the word spoken through Isaiah might be fulfilled: You shall indeed hear by hearing, and you will not understand' (Isa 6:9). 32.35 And he proceeds: 'These things He said when He had seen His glory, and He spoke about Him' (John 12:41). 32.36 And Peter, in the first epistle: 'Rejoice according to how you share in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may also rejoice in the revelation of His glory, exulting greatly' (1 Pet 4:13); 32.37 in the second: 'as all things pertaining to divine power have been granted to us for life and godliness through the knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and excellence' (2 Pet 1:3) instead of: 'the glory of the Only-Begotten, that of nature, that of wonders, that of the kingdom, and that of doxology itself, is similar and equal to the glory of the Father, from whom He has naturally and without separation been begotten, and He holds all things in Himself as the Only-Begotten, so that even having become flesh, He did not undergo any change or diminution.' 32.38 In this way also the three youths were not being consumed by the fire of Babylon, but were being consumed by longing for the Creator and Benefactor; rather than paying attention to the furnace surrounding them, prepared for the idol-worshippers in Gehenna, they submitted themselves to the Creation to give glory to the One appearing with them in the furnace, concerning whom it has been written, 'the vision of the fourth was like a Son of God' (Dan 3:25): 32.39 'Bless the Lord, all His works, O Lord; praise and exalt Him forever' (Ps 148:1, 13). 32.40 And while they were being reviled, he says, and while they were being struck against the children and the crowds because they were glorifying Jesus as God, saying, 'Hosanna in the highest; blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord' (Matt 21:9), he reminded them of the saying of the Scripture: 'Out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies You have perfected praise' (Ps 8:2), applying this word to himself and showing that glory is not to be brought to Him inappropriately. 32.41 And angels, he says,
after: The ages, if not the Only-begotten? Who are those who have exchanged his glory? They are those saying, 'glory to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit,' who also glorify him as a creature and not even as an eternal king.

Then he says to the same [people], 'in order that they might be without excuse, because having known God, they did not glorify him as God or gave thanks, but were made vain in their reasonings, and their foolish heart was darkened' (Romans 1:20). But what is the God who has been known yet not fully known by heretics and Jews and Greeks, if not the Word of God who appeared in the flesh?

And he shows to the Corinthians in the first letters that the Lord of glory is by nature [himself], thus writing: 'for if we had known, we would not have crucified the Lord of glory' (1 Cor 2:8), and also: 'that in the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bend and every tongue confess, that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father' (Phil 2:10-11), instead of [saying]: he exists in that paternal glory.

And again: 'for we see Jesus, him who was humbled, being crowned with glory and honor through the passion of death' (Hebrews 2:9). This is said out of order. For he says: we see Jesus, whom some think is being humbled through the passion of death, being crowned with glory and honor.

But he also calls him glory, even though being naturally a radiance of the paternal glory, through which he writes: 'the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory.' And he said God of the unspeakable incarnation, and Father of the unoriginate generation.

And again John says: 'we have beheld his glory, a glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth' (John 1:14).
